sections.heading: CHAPTER 6:  EQUIPMENT
sections.text:
Then straightway Robin Hood donned a fine steel coat of chain mail, over which he put a light jacket of Lincoln green. Upon his head he clapped a steel cap, and this he covered by one of soft white leather, in which stood a nodding cock’s plume. By his side hung a good broadsword of tempered steel, the bluish blade marked all over with strange figures of dragons, winged women, and what not.
―Howard Pyle, The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood (1883)
Starting Gear: If the optional rules for Social Class are not used to determine starting wealth (Chapter 1), then each player can simply select gear appropriate to the PC’s back story. If the total value is somewhere within the range of starting wealth for that class, it’s good. Certain groups more inclined to strict accountancy can of course roll for starting wealth and go shopping with it, but that’s not required. This applies to mundane equipment; masterwork, magical, and/or alchemical gear are handled using similar, parallel rules (see “Magic Items and Wealth,” below).

sections.heading: Armor
sections.text:
Armor types have been consolidated somewhat, as shown in the table below. These represent base armor types; it is possible to custom-design armor using special materials and properties, as outlined in the Appendices to this chapter (for example, “full plate” is made by simply applying a +1 AC bonus to plate armor).
Armor Type | Armor/ Shield Bonus | Max. Dex Bonus | Armor Check Penalty | Arcane Spell Failure | Speed Adjust-ment1 | Weight (lbs.) | Cost (gp)
Light armor |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Leather or “buff coat,” padded gambeson, arming doublet, etc. | +2 | +6 | 0 | 10% | 0 | 10 | 10
 |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
“Studded leather” | +3 | +5 | –1 | 15% | 0 | 15 | 25
Chain shirt (haubergeon), ring mail, light jack, tactical Kevlar vest, etc. | +4 | +4 | –2 | 20% | 0 | 20 | 75
Medium armor2 |  |  |  |  |  |  | 
Hide armor, wooden plateNAA | +4 | +4 | –3 | 20% | -5 ft. | 20 | 15
Scale byrnie, brigandine, coat-of-plates, plated jack, do-maru, etc. | +5 | +3 | –4 | 25% | -5 ft. | 25 | 100
Chainmail hauberk, breastplate, lamellar armor, plate carrier, etc. | +6 | +2 | –5 | 30% | -5 ft. | 30 | 250
Heavy armor3 |  |  |  |  |  |  |

Notes on armor
Movement speed penalties for all armor are eliminated if the armor check penalty is reduced to -0.Medium and heavy armor AC bonuses also apply as damage reduction, and as saving throw bonuses, against area-effect attacks (e.g., fireball).You cannot run in heavy armor unless the armor check penalty is -0.

sections.heading: Shields
sections.text:
As noted in Chapter 1, shield bonuses are equated to cover bonuses in these rules; they are not separate bonus types. Unlike cover provided by an obstacle, however, shield bonuses do not apply to your flat-footed AC.
Shields provide differing benefits depending upon your level of proficiency with them (Simple, Martial, or Exotic, as with weapons). Characters who are not proficient with shields gain a flat +1 cover bonus to AC (regardless of the type of shield), suffer a penalty to all attack rolls equal to the shield’s armor check penalty, and apply the shield’s armor check penalty to all Strength- and Dexterity-based skill checks.
If you use your shield as a weapon, you lose its AC bonus until your next turn. An enhancement bonus on a shield does not automatically improve the effectiveness of a shield bash made with it, but the shield can be made into a masterwork weapon or magical weapon in its own right.

sections.heading: Buckler/Dastana
sections.text:
The buckler, or “target,” is a very small shield that can be strapped to one arm and easily maneuvered. The dastana, or vambraces, are metal forearm guards worn with light armor. For the sake of simplicity, both devices share the same basic game rules. A buckler or pair of dastana weighs 3 lbs., has a -1 armor check penalty, and has a 5% arcane spell failure chance. It provides a base +1 cover bonus to AC (+0 vs. missiles).
Simple: You can use a buckler without suffering the non-proficiency penalties noted above. You gain the shield bonus to AC, but cannot use one hand as long as the buckler is carried. A character with only Simple proficiency gains no particular benefit from dastana.Martial: You can also use your shield arm to wield a weapon (whether you are using an off-hand weapon or using your off hand to help wield a two-handed weapon), but you take a –1 penalty on attack rolls while doing so. This penalty stacks with those that may apply for fighting with your off hand and for fighting with two weapons. In any case, if you use a weapon in your off hand, you lose the buckler's AC bonus until your next turn. You can cast a spell with somatic components using your shield arm, but you lose the buckler's AC bonus until your next turn.Exotic: You can freely use both hands with no penalty, and still gain the shield bonus to AC.

sections.heading: Shield, Heavy
sections.text:
A heavy shield is typically made of hide, wood, and/or steel, and is large enough to provide substantial protection. You strap the shield to your forearm and grip it with your hand; a heavy shield is so heavy that you can't use your shield hand for anything else. The hoplite aspis is a heavy bronze shield; the Norman kite shield is of wood, hide, and iron; the Roman scutum is of wood and leather; and the Zulu ishlangu (“war shield”) is of cowhide. 15 lbs., -2 check penalty, 15% arcane spell failure chance, partial cover (+2 to AC, +1 to Reflex saves).
Simple: You can use a heavy shield without suffering the normal non-proficiency penalty.Martial: In addition to the uses listed above, you receive an additional +2 AC bonus against missiles (total +4). You can bash with a shield as a one-handed weapon instead of using it for defense; it deals 1d4 bludgeoning damage (20/x2). A spiked heavy shield deals 1d6/19-20 piercing damage instead.Exotic: As martial proficiency, plus feat (Block Arrow; or Oversized Two-Weapon Fighting, enabling you to treat the heavy shield as if it were a light weapon for purposes of Two-Weapon Fighting).

sections.heading: Shield, Light
sections.text:
A light shield provides less area of coverage but is more quickly and easily brought to bear than a heavy shield. You strap the shield to your forearm and grip it with your hand. The Korean deungpae and Viking round shield are light wooden shields; the Moorish adarga and Zulu umbumbuluzo are of sturdy hide. A medieval knight’s “heater shield” could be of either steel or wood and leather. 5 lbs., -1 check penalty, 10% arcane spell failure chance, base +1 cover bonus to AC.
Simple: You can use a light shield without suffering the normal non-proficiency penalty.Martial: You carry other items in your shield hand, although you cannot use weapons or cast spells with it. You can bash an opponent with a light shield, using it as a light weapon. If you use your shield as a weapon, you lose its AC bonus until your next turn. It deals 1d3 bludgeoning damage (20/x2), or 1d4/19-20 with a central spike or sharpened rim.Exotic: As martial proficiency, plus feat (Block Arrow or Improved Shield Bash).

sections.heading: Shield, Tower
sections.text:
This massive wooden shield is nearly as tall as you are. 40 lbs., -10 check penalty, 50% arcane spell failure chance, maximum Dex bonus +2, cover (+4 to AC, +2 to Reflex saves).
Simple: You can use a tower shield without suffering the normal non-proficiency penalties (see Shields, above), although you still suffer a -2 penalty to attack rolls while using it.Martial: You do not suffer the standard -2 attack penalty for using the shield, and gain an additional +2 bonus to AC against missiles (+6 total). By giving up all actions for the round, you can take improved cover behind the shield (+8 AC, +4 to Reflex saves, evasion).Exotic: In addition to the AC bonus from the shield, you gain a +2 shield bonus to Reflex saves and Evasion (see Lightning Reflexes in Chapter 5). By giving up all actions for the round, you can take total cover behind your shield.

sections.heading: Weapons
sections.text:
There are other and natural causes tending toward a diminution of population, but nothing contributes so greatly to this end as the fact that no male or female Martian is ever voluntarily without a weapon of destruction.
―Edgar Rice Burroughs, A Princess of Mars (1912)
Many weapons have been re-categorized, and stats reassigned, from those listed in the core rules. Unlike in the core rules, in which weapons are individually classified as “simple,” “martial,” or “exotic,” these rules allow all weapons to be used with varying degrees of skill, depending on the level of proficiency of the wielder. The Simple Weapon Proficiency feat grants the Simple level of proficiency with all weapons. The Martial Weapon Proficiency feat grants Martial proficiency with all weapons within a particular weapons group (see below). The Exotic Weapon Proficiency feat grants the Exotic level of proficiency with a single weapon. Weapon groups are as follows:
Group | Weapons
Axes | Battleaxe, glaive, great axe, halberd, hand axe
Blades, Heavy | Arming sword, bastard sword, broadsword, estoc, greatsword, scimitar, scythe
Blades, Light | Dagger, cutlass, kukri, rapier, sickle, short sword, smallsword
Bludgeons | Great club, heavy club, heavy mace, light club, morning star, quarterstaff, sap, tonfa
Bows, etc. | Blowgun, hunting blowgun, longbow, short bow
Close weapons | Gauntlet, garotte, heavy shield, light shield, natural attacks, punching dagger, sap, spiked gauntlet, spiked shield, unarmed attacks, war fan
Crossbows | Hand crossbow, heavy crossbow, light crossbow, prodd
Flails and Whips | Chain whip, heavy flail, light flail, meteor hammer, pole flail, three-section staff, scourge, spiked chain, whip
Hammers and Picks | Heavy pick, great hammer, light hammer, light pick, Lucerne hammer, maul, military pick, warhammer
Polearms | Glaive, guisarme, halberd, lajatang, long spear, Lucerne hammer, mancatcher, morningstar, pole flail, ranseur
Slings | Atlatl, sling, staff sling
Spears | Harpoon, javelin, lance, long spear, ranseur, short spear, spear
Throwing Weapons | Bolas, boomerang, chakram, dagger, dart, hand axe, javelin, light hammer, net, rock

sections.heading: Weapon Properties
sections.text:
Brace: If you use a readied action to set a brace weapon against a charge, you deal double damage on a successful hit against a charging creature.
Disarm: When you use a disarm weapon, you get a +2 bonus on Combat Maneuver Checks to disarm an enemy.
Double Weapon: You can use a double weapon to fight as if fighting with two weapons, but if you do, you incur all the normal attack penalties associated with fighting with two weapons, just as if you were using a one-handed weapon and a light weapon.
Entangle: A successful attack also applies the entangled condition (Chapter 7) to the target. Unless otherwise noted, keeping an opponent entangled requires a CMB check on the wielder’s part each round after the initial one.
Feat: Some Exotic usages duplicate feats. You need not meet the prerequisites, but the feat applies only to the specific weapon in which you have the Exotic proficiency.
Finesse: You can use this weapon in conjunction with the Weapon Finesse feat (Chapter 5). All light weapons (q.v.) automatically have this property.
Light: Light melee weapons automatically have the finesse property (see above). They can be used in conjunction with the Two-Weapon Fighting feat (Chapter 5) with reduced penalties. A light weapon generally cannot be wielded two-handed; if done so, it does not gain 1½ times the wielder’s Strength bonus to damage.
Melee: The weapon cannot be effectively thrown without the Catch Off-Guard feat, unless it is also listed as a [throwing] or [projectile] weapon.
Nonlethal: These weapons deal nonlethal damage (see Combat).
One-handed: One-handed melee weapons apply your full Strength modifier to damage; if used in two hands, you can apply 1½ times your Strength bonus (if any) to damage.
Projectile: The weapon is used to fire projectiles, with the listed range increment. Each increment beyond the first applies a cumulative -2 penalty to attacks. Maximum range is ten such increments. Projectile weapons use the wielder’s Wisdom modifier for attacks, and may apply the user’s Strength modifier, depending on the weapon. Projectiles also generally must be reloaded between uses, requiring an action of some kind (see Reload, below).
Reach: You use a reach weapon to strike opponents 10 feet away, but you can't use it against an adjacent foe.
Reload: Most projectile weapons take time to reload, expressed as a number of move actions (Chapter 7)—generally your bonus move action and possibly one or more partial actions that would otherwise be used for iterative attacks. More proficient users can reload faster. It may also be possible for you to reload even more quickly by successful use of the Sleight of Hand skill (Chapter 4).
Throwing: The weapon can be thrown with the listed range increment; each increment beyond the first applies a cumulative -2 penalty to attacks. Maximum range is 5 increments. Throwing weapons use the wielder’s Strength modifier for attacks and damage; multiple weapons can be thrown in one round using the Sleight of Hand skill (Chapter 4).
Trip: If you are tripped during your own trip attempt, you can drop the weapon to avoid being tripped. Unlike non-trip weapons, weapons with the "trip" property allow you to apply weapon bonuses (enhancement, Weapon Specialization, etc.) and feat bonuses (Improved Trip, etc.) to your CBM when tripping. Note: You can attempt unarmed trips even without a free hand, using a foot.
Two-handed: Two-handed melee weapons require both hands to wield effectively. You apply 1½ times your Strength bonus (if any) to damage with two-handed weapons.
Multiple Options: Multiple options separated by an “and” are all available to a character with that level of proficiency. Multiple options with an “or” require the desired option to be chosen at the time the appropriate proficiency is taken. For weapons of this sort, the Exotic Weapon Proficiency can be selected multiple times, in order to gain multiple options. For example, the Exotic listing for the long spear reads as follows:
Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, feat (Lunge or Phalanx Fighter talent), reach; or two-handed melee, 2d6/x3, brace, reach.
A character with Exotic proficiency with the long spear can either (a) learn to use the Lunge feat with that weapon, or (b) learn to use the Phalanx Fighter talent with that weapon, or (c) learn to deal base 2d6 damage with the weapon (but gain none of the feat options, in that case). The brace and reach properties are gained no matter which option is selected. A character could potentially gain Exotic Weapon Proficiency with the long spear up to three times, in order to gain multiple options.

sections.heading: Axes
sections.text: Unless otherwise noted, axes deal slashing damage.

sections.heading: Axe, Battle
sections.text:
This is the famous one-handed Viking Axe. Weapons of this type include the Carpathian shepherd’s axe, Indian parashu, Khmer phkak, Moro panabas,  Scythian sagaris, and Viking Skeggøx (“bearded axe”); larger examples include the Danish axe, Norwegian peasant axe, and dwarven war axe. 4 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed melee, or one-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x3.Martial: One-handed melee, 1d8/x3 and two-handed melee, 1d10/x3.Exotic:  One-handed melee, 1d10/x3.

sections.heading: Axe, Great
sections.text:
Includes all heavy, two-handed axes without reach, such as the bardiche, the sparth axe (“Gallowglass axe”), the “Jeddart stave,” and the Lochaber axe. 9 lbs.
Simple: Two-handed melee, -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x3.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d12/x3.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 2d8/x3.

sections.heading: Axe, Hand
sections.text:
An incredibly versatile weapon and tool, the hand axe can be thrown or used in melee, and can be used to make tripping attacks. Includes the hatchet, the Algonquian tomahawk, the Congolese nzappa-zap, the Frankish francisca, the Japanese ono, the Malay kapak siam, and the American Tomahawk Company VTAC. Also use these stats for a meat cleaver (using the x4 critical multiplier for Exotic proficiency), or the D&D thrombashSSt and ice axeFB. 2 lbs.
Simple: One-handed melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x2.Martial: Light melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x3, trip.Exotic: Light melee and throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/x3, disarm, trip; or light melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x4.

sections.heading: Glaive
sections.text:
A glaive is a simple blade, mounted to the end of a pole. Similar reach weapons include the French fauchard, Japanese naginata, Korean woldo, Muscovite sovnya, Swedish svärdstav, Thai ngao.  The pollaxe, couteau de brèche, voulge, longaxeARG, and sugliinFB can all be treated as glaives. The “tri-point double-edged sword” of Kung Fu movies, while more exotic-looking, is functionally identical to a glaive; one might also consider an Aztec tepoztopili as a glaive rather than a spear.
The Exotic trip use can be accomplished by adding a hook to the back, creating a glaive-guisarme; another example is the Chinese guandao or the horsechopperUE of Golarion. The added damage option for Exotic use supersedes the heavy poleaxeCW. An Exotic wielder with Shorten Grip option and the Two-Weapon Fighting feat can use a glaive as a double weapon, striking with the butt as if it were a staff. 4 lbs.
Simple: Two-handed melee, -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x3, reach.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, reach.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, feat (Shorten Grip), reach, trip; or two-handed melee, 2d6/x3, reach.

sections.heading: Halberd
sections.text:
The halberd consists of a small axe blade topped with a spike, mounted on a shaft. It has a hook on the back side of the axe blade, used for snagging mounted combatants. A halberd can be used to perform trip attacks, and can be braced against an enemy charge; exotic proficiency supersedes the dwarven warpikeRS and the ritiikFB. The Chinese ji is essentially similar. 6 lbs, slashing or piercing damage.
Simple: Two-handed melee, -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x2, brace.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, brace, trip.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, brace, feat (Improved Trip or Lunge), trip.

sections.heading: Estoc
sections.text:
The estoc was a two-handed thrusting sword, almost like a giant two-handed rapier, designed for fighting against mail or plate armor. Over 4 ft. long, 4 lbs., piercing damage.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 2d4/19-20.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 2d4/18-20.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 2d4/18-20 plus feat (Scything Blow); or one-handed melee, 2d4/18-20.

sections.heading: Scimitar
sections.text:
Any single-handed, curved sword that is lighter than a broadsword but longer than a cutlass can be considered a scimitar; this includes the cavalry saber and Mameluke sword, the Burmese dha, the Chinese dao, the Indian tulwar, the Persian shamshir, the Polish hussar szabla, the Russian Cossack shashka, and the Turkish yataghan and kilij. The curve allows more momentum to be focused on a single point along the blade, accounting for the weapon’s excellent critical range; with Exotic proficiency, a “drawing cut” producing bleeding wounds is perfected. 2.5 lbs., slashing damage. For characters who wish to fight with a pair of sabers, the cutlass (q.v.) is designed for that use.

Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/19-20.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/18-20.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d6/18-20 and feat (Bleeding Strike).

sections.heading: Scythe
sections.text:
A scythe consists of an S-shaped wooden shaft with a long, curved blade set on it. Although capable of dealing horrendous wounds, it is a clumsy weapon except in well-trained hands. The two-handed Dacian falx is an example. 5 lbs., slashing damage. A longer war scythe is represented using the guisarme statistics (see Polearms). You can use the scythe stats for an ogre hookUE, or for a mercurial greatswordS&F (like Terminus Est from Gene Wolfe’s Book of the New Sun).

Simple: Two-handed with -4 competence penalty to attacks melee, 2d4/x3.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 2d4/x3, trip.Exotic:  Two-handed melee, 2d4/x4, trip.

sections.heading: Sword, Arming
sections.text:
The arming sword is a multipurpose cutting and thrusting weapon, generally with a straight blade approximately 3 feet long. This is the D&D “longsword,” although the historical European longsword was in fact a bastard sword (q.v.). The knight’s sword, the side-sword, the Walloon sword, the Landsknecht’s Katzbalger, the “mortuary sword” used in the English Civil War, the Viking sword, the Chinese jian, the Roman spatha, and the Sudanese kaskara, are all represented by arming sword statistics under these rules. Exotic wielders become more adept with the point, rapier-like, and have more finesse overall; this supersedes the Aldori dueling swordAG, the elven thinbladeRW, and the elven longbladeDr351. 2 lbs., slashing and piercing damage.
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/19-20.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d8/19-20.Exotic:  One-handed melee, 1d8/18-20, Finesse; or one-handed melee, 1d8/19-20 and 1d12/19-20 vs. opponents of size Large or larger.

sections.heading: Sword, Bastard
sections.text:
The bastard sword is similar to an arming sword or scimitar, but with a 4-foot blade and longer handle allowing better leverage with two-handed blows; it is often referred to as a “hand-and-a-half sword.” This includes the Renaissance “long sword” and the Portuguese montante. Curved bastard swords include the German Kriegsmesser and the Chinese dadao. Smaller claymores and short-handled Thracian rhomphaia can also be treated as bastard swords. For the sake of convenience, the Aztec macuahuitl can use these stats, especially if the Bleeding Strike feat is also selected. 4 lbs., slashing damage.
Exotic proficiency simulates the Japanese katana, the great scimitarSSt, the elven curve bladeUE, the elven courtbladeRW, and the so-called “falchion” as described in the core rules.

Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/19-20.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20; and one-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/19-20.Exotic:  One-handed melee (1d10/19-20), and two-handed melee (1d10/18-20 and finesse), or special (1d10/19-20 and 2d8/19-20 against Large or larger opponents).

sections.heading: Sword, Broad
sections.text:
True broadswords—such as the Scottish broadsword, the Chinese “ox-tailed sword” (niuweidao, or “nine—ring broadsword” in Pathfinder), German Große Messer, Iberian falcata, Indian pata, Rajput khanda, and Venetian schiavona—use the sword’s weight to add power to the blow. The weapon’s balance is such, however, that it cannot be effectively wielded in two hands. A broadsword is generally fitted with a basket hilt, providing a +2 enhancement bonus against disarm attempts. Hangers and backswords can be treated as broadswords. 3 lbs., slashing damage.
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 2d4/19-20.Martial:  One-handed melee, 2d4/19-20.Exotic:  One-handed melee, 2d4/19-20/x3.

sections.heading: Sword, Great
sections.text:
The great sword includes any two-handed slashing sword, including the Chinese changdao or miaodao, German Landsnechte’s Zweihänder/Bidenhänder, Japanese no-dachi (and the nagamaki, for that matter), six-foot Korean ssangsudo, Scottish claymore, and D&D great falchionSSt. 6 lbs., slashing damage.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 2d6/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 2d6/19-20.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 2d6/19-20 and 3d6/19-20 against Large or larger opponents.

sections.heading: Cutlass
sections.text:
A small cutlass includes any slashing weapon larger than a simple knife but smaller than a full-sized sword. Examples include the machete, the Arabic jambiya, Chinese “butterfly sword,” Filipino bolo, German Dusack, Greek kopis, Indonesian golok, Japanese wakizashi, Maasai seme, Malaysian parang, Old English seax, Sumatran klewang, Yoruba ida, and the goblin dogslicerUE of Golarion. Exotic proficiency replicates the sawtooth sabrePC and the Dervish Dance featPC. 2 lbs., slashing damage.
Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x2.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/19-20.Exotic:  Light melee, 1d6/18-20; or 1d8/19-20 and one-handed thrown (10 ft.), 1d6/19-20.

sections.heading: Dagger
sections.text:
Any edged weapon with a blade about a foot in length―including the American Bowie knife and marine KA-BAR, English Fairbairn-Sykes fighting knife, French poignard, Indian bichuwa, Indonesian kris, Japanese tantō, Roman pugio, Scottish dirk, Swiss baselard, etc. You get a +2 bonus on Sleight of Hand skill checks made to conceal a dagger on your person. 1 lb., piercing (secondary slashing) damage (piercing only, if thrown).

Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/19-20.Martial: Light melee, 1d4/19-20, and light throwing (10 ft.), 1d4/19-20.Exotic: Light melee, 1d4/19-20 and sneak attack +1d6, and light throwing (10 ft.) 1d4/19-20; or light melee (1d4/19-20) and light throwing (10 ft.), 1d4/19-20/x3.
Synergy: If you have Exotic dagger proficiency and also have the sneak attack class feature, the effects stack. In addition, if your base sneak attack ability (not including this feature) is at least +7d6, you gain an additional +1d6 when using a dagger (+9d6 total). This is a specific exception to the general rule capping sneak attack damage at +1d6/2 levels (rounded up), and emulates the Knife Master’s sneak stabAPG.

sections.heading: Sickle
sections.text:
The sickle, derived from the grain cutting tool, is a wooden handle with a short, curved blade. Examples include the Indian aruval, Japanese kama, smaller (one-handed) Dacian falx, Madurese celurit, Tamil aruval, and Zande makraka. Other hooked slashing weapons, such as the common kaiser blade (“some folks call it a sling blade”), Abyssinian shotel, Chilean corvo, Chinese hook sword (shuan gou) and “double chicken saber,” Ngombe ngulu sword, or smaller Egyptian khopesh can also be represented as a sickle, as can the eagle’s clawSSt and the Dothraki “arakh” from the Game of Thrones TV show. The Napalese kukri (“Ghurka knife”) and Indonesian and Sumatran karambit are insufficiently different to warrant separate statistics (Cf. Ramrowan in The Man from Nowhere, or The Assassin in The Raid 2). Also reference the Ustaše strobsjek (with a glove fitting). 1-2 lbs., slashing damage.
Simple:  Light melee, 1d6/x2.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/19-20, trip (sickle); or light melee, 1d4/18-20 (kukri).Exotic:  Light melee, 1d6/18-20, disarm, trip.

sections.heading: Sword, Rapier
sections.text:
The rapier is a long, thin sword, usually with no cutting edge; variants include the Spanish espada ropera. A rapier cannot be effectively wielded in two hands. 2 lbs., piercing damage.
Simple: One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/19-20.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/18-20, Finesse.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d6/18-20, Disarm, Finesse, and feat (Lunge).

The smallsword (also court sword, French colichemarde, épée de cour, or dress sword) is a light weapon designed for thrusting which evolved out of the longer and heavier rapier of the late Renaissance. It is identical to the rapier, except it is a light weapon instead of a one-handed weapon; this supersedes the elven lightbladeRW. 1 lb., piercing damage.

sections.heading: Sword, Short
sections.text:
In the hands of Roman Legionnaires, the Gladius became the most destructive weapon until the advent of the firearm. More soldiers died of wounds inflicted by the gladius than were killed by any other weapon in antiquity.	―Richard A. Gabriel,
The Great Armies of Antiquity (2002)
This category of weapon includes any thrusting blade longer than a dagger, but shorter than a full-sized sword; the Roman gladius is the defining example. Other similar weapons, such as the Filipino balasiong, the Greek xiphos, the Somali billao, the Swiss degen, and the U.S. Model 1832 foot artillery sword, are also treated as short swords. 1 lb., piercing damage.

Simple: One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/19-20.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/19-20.Exotic:  Light melee, 1d6/19-20/x3.

sections.heading: Bludgeons
sections.text: As their name implies, unless otherwise noted all bludgeons deal bludgeoning damage.

sections.heading: Club, Great
sections.text:
The great club is simply a heavy, two-handed club. Fancy versions might be bound in iron and set with metal studs, like the Japanese tetsubo or kanabo. 6 lbs.
Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x4.

sections.heading: Club, Heavy
sections.text:
One of the most basic and effective weapons of all. Heavier bludgeons, such as an Iroquois ball-headed or gunstock war club (as in Michael Mann’s Last of the Mohicans), a baseball bat, an Irish shillelagh, a Japanese bokken (wooden practice sword) ―or even a pickaxe handle (as in Eastwood’s Pale Rider) or length of metal pipe―fall under this category. 2.5 to 4 lbs.
Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x2.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x3.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d6/x3, Feat (Staggering Strike), and one-handed throwing, 1d6/x2, 10 ft.

sections.heading: Club, Light
sections.text:
Any lightweight bludgeon, such as a belaying pin, singlestick, WW1 trench raiding club, French canne de combat, Japanese hanbo or jō, Maori patu (including the mere) or kotiate, South African knobkierrie, Filipino baston (yantok, or “escrima stick”), etc., is treated as a light club. Light clubs do not provide sufficient weight and leverage to gain additional damage from being used two-handed. Most styles featured training in Two-Weapon Fighting (such as with the paired sticks or the Philippine knife-and-stick) or throwing (such as the Zulu iwisa). 1 to 2 lbs.
Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d4/x2.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/x2 and feat (Two-Weapon Fighting); or light melee and light throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x2.Exotic:  Light melee, 1d6/x2, feat (Two-Weapon Fighting); and light throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x2, feat (Far Shot).
Synergy: If you have at least Martial proficiency with light clubs and also Exotic proficiency with light flails, you can use a dan bong (Korean rope stick) as a light club or as a light flail, depending on how you swing it. If you have the Improved Grapple feat, you can also perform grapples (locks) using the dan bong.  Until you do so, the weapon appears to be nothing more than a light club to anyone lacking those proficiencies. A dan bong can also be used as a cord garrot (see under Close Weapons, below).

sections.heading: Mace, Heavy
sections.text:
A mace is made up of an ornate metal head attached to a simple wooden or metal shaft. The Indian gada and shishpar and the Russian pernach and shestopyor are examples of flanged maces. The Japanese kanabo and Chinese chui are also essentially maces.
The one-handed “morningstar” in the core rules is treated as a heavy mace (use the increased damage option for Exotic proficiency and assume damage is bludgeoning and piercing); the medieval morning star (q.v.) was a typically two-handed pole weapon. Exotic use also replicates the warmaceCW, warscepterDD, and tigerskull clubFB. 2 lbs. to 6 lbs.

Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d8/x2.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d8/x3.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d8/x3, feat (Crushing Blow); or one-handed melee, 1d12/x3; or one-handed melee, 1d8/x4.

sections.heading: Morning Star
sections.text:
This is an infantry weapon in the form of a thick wooden shaft 6 to 8 feet in length (one example in Vienna is 7 feet 9 inches long), slightly fluted toward the top, with a spiked head and topped with a stout iron spike. The French plançon a picot, English “holy water sprinkler,” and Scottish brogit staff are examples; longer Aztec macuahuitl or Maori terbutje can also be treated as morning stars. For a shorter handled, one-handed weapon like the one described in the D&D and Pathfinder rules, use the stats for a heavy mace (q.v.), but change the damage type to bludgeoning and piercing. 10 lbs, bludgeoning and piercing damage.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x3.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, brace.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, brace, and feat (Lunge).

sections.heading: Sap
sections.text:
The sap, or blackjack, is a sandbag or cushioned weight, often on a spring handle, used to bludgeon opponents unconscious. 1 lb.
Simple: Light melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2 nonlethal.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/x3 nonlethal.Exotic: Light melee, 1d6/x3 nonlethal, feat (Knockout Blow).

sections.heading: Staff, Pole
sections.text:
Generally used as a training weapon to develop strength and power when using smaller staves, a long staff, or “pole” like the ones used in Ip Man 3, can be used as a weapon on its own.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2 bludgeoning, reach.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d6/x3 bludgeoning, reach.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3 bludgeoning, reach.

sections.heading: Staff, Quarter
sections.text:
The simple staff, whether shod and weighted like the English quarterstaff, or simply made of strong bamboo or other light wood (as the Chinese gun, Japanese bo staff, or Korean gonbang), is a useful double weapon. 3 lbs. The Maori taiaha is essentially a double weapon, with a quarterstaff for one end and a short spear for the other.
Simple: Two-handed melee, 1d6/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee double weapon, 1d6/x2, feat (Two Weapon Fighting).Exotic: Two-handed melee double weapon, 1d6/x3, feats (Two-Weapon Fighting and Two Weapon Defense); or one-handed melee weapon, 1d6/x3.

sections.heading: Tonfa
sections.text:
Any light bludgeoning weapon with a side handle or prong in order to catch opponents’ weapons and allow for variant grips (including a billy club) can be treated as a tonfa.  For example, a sai is a metal spike flanked by a pair of prongs used to trap an enemy's weapon; though pointed, a sai is used primarily to bludgeon foes and to disarm weapons, so it falls into this category for the sake of simplicity (as does the jutte). The aklys, owing to the side hook, can also be treated as a tonfa, as can the notched Maori wahaika. However, it is attached to a 20-ft. cord, and can be retrieved after throwing as a partial action. 2 lbs.
Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/x2.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/x2, disarm, trip.Exotic: Light melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x3, disarm, trip; and retrieve after throwing as an immediate action.

sections.heading: Bows
sections.text:
This group is also used as a catch-all for projectile weapons (such as the blowgun) that don’t belong anywhere else. Unless otherwise noted, they deal piercing damage.
Special: Standard short bows and longbows are constructed for a person of average Strength (10-11). Strength penalties to damage apply, but not bonuses due to higher Strength unless a composite bow is used. Composite bows have a greater “pull,” and require a minimum Strength score to use. A wielder meeting or exceeding that minimum can add his or her Strength bonus to damage. Composite bows also add 10 ft. to the range increments shown.

sections.heading: Blowgun, Light
sections.text:
Blowguns are generally used to deliver debilitating (but rarely fatal) poisons from a distance. They are nearly silent when fired. Blowgun darts do not allow the user to apply a Strength bonus to damage. The smaller Japanese fukiya blowgun is a simple weapon appropriate for ninjas; 2 lbs, piercing damage.

Simple: One-handed projectile (10 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1, reload 2 move actions.Martial: One-handed projectile (10 ft.), 1, reload 1 move action.Exotic: One-handed projectile (10 ft.), 1, reload 1 swift action.

sections.heading: Blowgun, Hunting
sections.text:
The longer South American and Cherokee blowguns have a much longer range, with the disadvantage of being 6 to 9 feet long and unwieldy. Blowgun darts do not allow the user to apply a Strength bonus to damage. 3 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (30 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d2, reload 1 full round.Martial: Two-handed projectile (30 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d3, reload 2 move actions.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (30 ft.), 1d4, reload 1 move action.

sections.heading: Bow, Long
sections.text:
Six-foot bows like the English longbow and the Japanese daikyu fall under this heading. The daikyu’s grip was off-center, allowing it to be used while mounted (simulated here by Exotic proficiency). 3 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (100 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x3, reload 2 move actions.Martial: Two-handed projectile (100 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload 1 move action.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (100 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload 1 swift action, or 1 move action if used while mounted (daikyu).

sections.heading: Bow, Short
sections.text:
A short bow is about 3 feet in length; examples include the Mongol bow and the Japanese hankyu. You can use a short bow while mounted. 2 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (60 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x3, reload 1 move action.Martial: Two-handed projectile (60 ft.), 1d6/x3, reload 1 swift action.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (60 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload 1 free action, or reload 1 swift action (and no Concentration check needed for use—see Chapter 4) if fired while on a moving mount or pitching ship’s deck, while flying, etc.).

sections.heading: Dagger, Punching
sections.text:
A punching dagger's blade is often attached to a horizontal handle that projects out from the fist when held. The Indian katara is an example of a punching dagger, as is the riverboat gambler’s “push knife.” The Malaysian siangham and Chinese emeici, and the fingerbladeSSt and Gehennan lancetPnH, can essentially be treated as punching daggers as well. 1 lb., piercing damage.
Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/x3.Martial: Light melee, 1d4/x3 and feat (Deft Blow).Exotic: Light melee, 1d4/x3 and feats (Deft Blow, Hammer the Gap); or light melee, 1d6/x3 and feat (Deft Blow).

sections.heading: Fan, War
sections.text:
The Japanese war fan (gunsen) is a metal fan, usually with sharpened edges, that can be concealed as a normal court fan or small club. 2 lbs., slashing or bludgeoning damage.
Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/x2.Martial: Light melee, 1d6/19-20.Exotic: Light melee, 1d6/19-20 and thrown (5 ft.).

sections.heading: Garrote, Cord
sections.text:
This is nothing more than a simple strangling cord, such as a Thuggee’s silken garrote or a Mafioso’s “rope.” In order for you to use a garrote, your opponent must be helpless or unaware of you. You must make a grapple check (though you avoid the –4 penalty for not having two hands free) to successfully begin garroting your opponent. Negligible weight; special damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d4 on grapple.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d4 on grapple, feat (Throat Punch).Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d4 on grapple, improved grab, feats (Improved Grapple, Throat Punch).
Synergy: If you also have the Vital Strike feat, that damage applies to garrote damage; this is true of the wire garrote as well.

sections.heading: Garrote, Wire
sections.text:
A garrote is a length of wire with wooden handles at both ends. The wire is placed across a victim's throat and crossed behind the neck; when the handles are pulled tight, the garrote strangles him. It is otherwise similar to a strangling cord (see garrote, cord). Negligible weight; slashing damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d6 on grapple.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d6/19-20 on grapple, feat (Throat Punch).Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d6/19-20 on grapple, feats (Improved Grapple, Throat Punch).

sections.heading: Gauntlet
sections.text:
Any armored glove or other means of adding weight and/or hardness to a basic fist (brass knuckles, or even a simple roll of quarters) uses these statistics (e.g., the cestus is a glove of leather or thick cloth that covers the wielder from mid-finger to mid-forearm, reinforced with metal plates over the fingers). An armored gauntlet or cestus gives you a –2 penalty on all precision-based tasks involving that hand (such as opening locks). 1 lb., bludgeoning damage.

Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/x2.Martial:  Light melee, 1d4/19-20.Exotic: Light melee, 1d6/19-20, feats/class features applying to unarmed attacks also apply to your gauntlets (q.v.).

sections.heading: Gauntlet, Spiked
sections.text:
Adding spikes to a gauntlet or cestus allows more damaging attacks, at the cost of added weight. Treat the Indian bagh nakh and 2 lbs, piercing damage.
Simple:  Light melee, 1d4/19-20.Martial:  Light melee, 1d6/19-20.Exotic: Light melee, 1d6/19-20 and feat (Hammer the Gap).

sections.heading: Sap
sections.text: See full descriptions under “Bludgeons.”

sections.heading: Unarmed Attack
sections.text:
A non-proficient character can make flailing blows without a weapon; these blows provoke attacks of opportunity. At the Simple level of proficiency, unarmed attacks are basic punches, unable to deal lethal damage but not provoking attacks of opportunity. Kicks, elbows, etc. can be added to the repertoire at the Martial level, and at the Exotic level of proficiency the character is a skilled martial artist or brawler.

Simple: Light unarmed (melee), 1d3 nonlethal.Martial: Light unarmed (melee), 1d4/19-20 nonlethal.Exotic: Light unarmed (melee), 1d4/19-20 lethal or nonlethal, and your unarmed attacks are treated both as manufactured weapons and as natural weapons for the purpose of spells and effects that enhance or improve either manufactured weapons or natural weapons.
Synergy: If you also have the Improved Weapon Maneuvers feat, you can make unarmed parry, bind, and disarm attempts (and sunder attempts against wooden weapons) as if you were armed.
Source: Martial proficiency in unarmed attacks supersedes the Improved Unarmed Strike feat; Exotic proficiency subsumes the Superior Unarmed Strike featToB.

sections.heading: Crossbows
sections.text:
Crossbows work similarly to bows, except their Strength is mechanical (through winding) rather than limited by the user’s Strength. Default mechanical strength scores are 12 (+1 damage) for a hand crossbow, 16 (+3) for a light crossbow, and 20 (+5) for a heavy crossbow. Crossbows can be constructed with higher mechanical strength scores (see “Spring Steel” under special materials, below), but they are expensive and difficult to produce.
Some crossbows can be fired one-handed (as shown in the individual descriptions), but all of them generally require two hands to reload.
Exotic Proficiency: If you have Exotic proficiency with a crossbow that is loaded and in hand, any time you are hit with a ranged attack, you can fire that crossbow at your attacker as an attack of opportunity.
Repeating Crossbows: Repeating crossbows like the Chinese chu-ke-nu hold 5 crossbow bolts. As long as it holds bolts, you can reload it by pulling the reloading lever (a free action). Loading a new case of 5 bolts is a full-round action (regardless of your level of proficiency) that provokes attacks of opportunity. Repeating crossbows have a mechanical Strength score 4 lower than normal (1d6+1 damage for light repeating crossbows, 1d8+3 for heavy repeating crossbows). Hand crossbows (and prods) do not have repeating versions.
Standard crossbows deal piercing damage; the prodd deals bludgeoning damage instead.

sections.heading: Crossbow, Hand
sections.text:
You can draw a hand crossbow back by hand. You can shoot, but not load, a hand crossbow with one hand at no penalty. You can shoot a hand crossbow with each hand, but you take a penalty on attack rolls as if attacking with two light weapons. Reloading takes 2 hands. 2 lbs.
Simple: Light projectile (30 ft.), 1d4+1/19-20, reload 2 move actions.Martial:  Light projectile (30 ft.), 1d4+1/19-20, reload 1 move action.Exotic: Light projectile (30 ft.), 1d4+1/19-20, reload 1 swift action.

sections.heading: Crossbow, Heavy
sections.text:
The heavy crossbow, or arbalest, is drawn back by turning a small winch. Normally, operating a heavy crossbow requires two hands. However, you can shoot, but not load, a heavy crossbow with one hand at a –4 penalty on attack rolls. 8 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (120 ft.), 1d8+5/19-20, reload 1 full round (provokes attacks of opportunity).Martial:  Two-handed projectile (120 ft.), 1d8+5/19-20, reload 2 move actions.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (120 ft.), 1d8+5/19-20, feat (Fell Shot or Vital Stike*), reload 1 move action.
*	If you already have the Vital Strike feat, you gain the effects of the Powerful Bolt fighter talent when firing a heavy crossbow.

sections.heading: Crossbow, Light
sections.text:
You draw a light crossbow back by pulling a lever. Normally, operating a light crossbow requires two hands. However, you can shoot, but not load, a light crossbow with one hand at a –2 penalty on attack rolls. You can shoot a light crossbow with each hand, but you take a penalty on attack rolls as if attacking with two weapons. 4 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (80 ft.), 1d6+3/19-20, reload 2 move actions.Martial:  Two-handed projectile (80 ft.), 1d6+3/19-20, reload 1 move action.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (80 ft.), 1d6+3/19-20, feat (Insightful Strike or Deft Blow), reload 1 move action.

sections.heading: Prodd
sections.text:
The prodd is, in essence, a small hand catapult that fires sling bullets rather than bolts. Normally, operating a prodd requires two hands. However, you can shoot, but not load, a prodd with one hand at no penalty on attack rolls. Like a light crossbow, a prod has an effective mechanical Strength of 15. 4 lbs.

Simple: Light projectile (80 ft.), 1d4+2/x2, reload 2 move actions.Martial: Light projectile (60 ft.), 1d4+2/x2, reload 1 move action.Exotic: Light projectile (80 ft.), 1d4+2/x2, reload 1 move action.

sections.heading: Flails and Whips
sections.text: Historical Note: The historical use of a heavy or light flail as an actual combat weapon is somewhat dubious. In addition, it should be noted that the primary functions of nunchaku involve tradition (not to mention impressive style and flash), rather than combat effectiveness; the same is true of the three-section staff. However, because of the enormous popularity of these weapons in cinema, gaming, and traditional martial arts (and given the author grew up with Bruce Lee movies), they have been given effective combat statistics in these rules.

sections.heading: Chain, Spiked
sections.text:
Essentially a double chain whip (q.v.)―heavier, with bladed and/or weighted tips at both ends, and it can be gripped anywhere along the chain. Includes the Japanese kusari-fundo (manrikigusari). Exotic usage includes the kawanagaOA. 5 lbs, bludgeoning and piercing damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8, entangle.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d8, entangle, finesse.Exotic: Two-handed melee double weapon, 1d8/1d8; and two-handed melee reach weapon 1d8 (shift grip as swift action); disarm, entangle, finesse, trip.

sections.heading: Flail, Heavy
sections.text:
A heavy flail consists of a long handle with a spiked metal striking end―rather like the end of a morning star―attached by means of a chain or swivel. 10 lbs, bludgeoning damage. 6 lbs, bludgeoning (secondary piercing) damage.

Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/19-20.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, disarm, trip.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, disarm, trip; and two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, disarm and special (cannot be parried or redirected; not affected by Combat Expertise or defensive fighting).

sections.heading: Flail, Light
sections.text:
In addition to the familiar image of a handle with a spiked ball at the end of a chain (a “horseman’s flail”), the light flail includes any one-handed martial bludgeon with a rope or swivel, such as a grain thresher, a set of nunchaku, or a “flindbar.” 2 to 3 lbs, bludgeoning (and possibly piercing) damage.
Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x2, with a -4 nonproficiency penalty.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x2, disarm.Exotic: Light melee, 1d8/19-20, disarm.

Synergy: Nunchaku can be used as a cord garrot (see Close Weapons, above), and in fact are illegal in Germany for that reason.

sections.heading: Flail, Pole
sections.text:
This is simply a long heavy flail with reach, forming a sort of polearm. An example is the Japanese chigiriki. 12 lbs., bludgeoning (secondary piercing) damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/19-20, reach.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, reach, trip.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, feat (Crushing Blow), reach, trip.

sections.heading: Hammer, Meteor
sections.text:
This weapon is a spherical or conical weight attached to a 15-foot rope. This weapon includes the rope dart or jōhyō and the dorn-dergarPC. 6-7 lbs, bludgeoning damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x2, finesse, reach.Martial:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/19-20, entangle, finesse, reach; and one-handed throwing, 1d4/19-20, retrieve by means of rope (adjust grip as partial action).Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, disarm, entangle, finesse, reach, trip; and two-handed melee, 1d10/19-20, trip (adjust grip as an immediate action; this supersedes the Darting Viper featPC.

sections.heading: Scourge
sections.text:
The scourge is a short, heavy, multi-tailed whip, capable of leaving bleeding wounds. The “cat-o’-nine tails” uses the scourge statistics, as does the (single-tailed) Cossack nagaikaMW. 2 lbs, slashing damage.
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x3, disarm.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d6/x3, disarm, trip, feat (Bleeding Strike).

sections.heading: Staff, Three-Section
sections.text:
The three-section staff (sanjiegun or sansetsukon) is a flail weapon that consists of three wooden or metal staves connected by metal rings or rope. A more complicated version of the light flail, the staves can be spun to gather momentum resulting in a powerful blow. 5 lbs, bludgeoning damage. More proficient wielders can use both ends simultaneously, as a double weapon; these stats therefore cover the 3.5 edition “dire flail.”

Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3; and two-handed melee double weapon, 1d6/x3.Exotic: Two-handed melee weapon, 1d10/x3, disarm, feat (Lunge), finesse, trip; and two-handed melee double weapon, 1d8/x3, finesse, feat (Two-Weapon Fighting).

sections.heading: Whip
sections.text:
The whip is treated as a melee weapon with 15-foot reach, though you don't threaten the area into which you can make an attack. Using a whip provokes an attack of opportunity, just as if you had used a ranged weapon, unless you have Exotic proficiency with it (Exotic whip proficiency also supersedes the Whip MasteryUC feat).
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d3 nonlethal, finesse, reach.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d3 nonlethal, finesse, reach.Exotic: Light melee, 1d3 lethal or nonlethal (your choice each attack), disarm, reach, trip.

Synergy: If you also have the Ranged Maneuvers feat (q.v.), you can use a whip to grasp an unattended Small or Tiny object within 15 ft. and pull that object into your square. To do so, you must hit AC 10 with a melee touch attack. Further, you can use the whip to grasp onto an object within 10 ft., using 5 feet of your whip as if it were a grappling hook, allowing you to use the rest of your whip to swing on like a rope. As an immediate action, you can release the object your whip is grasping, but you cannot use the whip to attack while the whip is grasping an object.
If you have the Improved Grapple feat (q.v.), you gain the ability to grapple using your whip. To do so, use the normal grapple rules with the following changes.
Attack: You cannot use your whip to attack while you are using it to grapple an opponent.Damage: When dealing damage to your grappled opponent, you deal your whip’s weapon damage rather than your unarmed damage.Free Hands: You take no penalty on your combat maneuver check for having fewer than two hands free when you use your whip to grapple.
These synergy effects supersede the Whip Mastery and Greater Whip Mastery featsUC.

sections.heading: Whip, Chain
sections.text:
Any one-handed flexible, whip-like weapon with a handle at one end and a sharp edge or tip fits under the category of “chain whips.” Examples include the scorpion whip, the whip-dagger, the kau sin ke, the urumi of the Punjab, the nine-section whipUC, and the bladed scarf of VarisiaPC. 3 lbs, Slashing.

The Japanese kusarigama is a double weapon equivalent to a sickle (q.v.) for one end and a chain whip for the other. The chijirikiOA is a double weapon combining the chain whip and the short spear (q.v.).
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2, reach.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/19-20, entangle, finesse, reach.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d8/18-20, disarm, entangle, finesse, reach, trip.

sections.heading: Hammers and Picks
sections.text: Historical Note: Warhammers and picks were generally combined or even indistinguishable from one another; for the sake of game continuity, they are listed separately here. Unless otherwise noted, all hammers deal bludgeoning damage; picks deal piercing damage.

sections.heading: Hammer, Great
sections.text:
Appearing as a weapon only in fantasy, a great hammer is a massive, two-handed weapon akin to the thing used in Conan the Barbarian, or the earth breakerUE in the Golarion setting. 16 lbs.
Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 2d6/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 2d6/x3.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 2d6/x3, feat (Staggering Strike).

sections.heading: Hammer, Light
sections.text:
The light hammer is an especially short-handled, blunt-headed warhammer, balanced for throwing. 2 lbs.
Simple: Light melee and throwing (10 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x2.Martial:  Light melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d4/x3.Exotic:  Light melee and throwing (20 ft.), 1d4/x3, feat (Staggering Strike).

sections.heading: Hammer, War
sections.text:
The historical warhammer, including the horseman’s hammer, was a lightweight, long-handled weapon designed to damage even armored opponents. The small, pronged hammer head is often backed with a military pick. Similar weapons such as the Fijian totokia (“pineapple club”) can also use these statistics. 2.5 lbs.

Simple: One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x3.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d8/x3.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d8/x3, feat (Crushing Blow).

sections.heading: Lucerne Hammer
sections.text:
This polearm has both a pronged hammer head for crushing blows and a spiked head for piercing mail; attacks against plate armor are made with the hammer. The long haft allows the wielder to put great force behind the head of this weapon. The earlier bec de corbin is essentially similar; the dwarven long-hammerARG and the ramhammerPnH can be treated as Lucerne hammers. 10 lbs, piercing and bludgeoning damage.

Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 2d4/x3, reach.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, reach.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 2d6/x3, feat (Scything Blow), reach.

sections.heading: Maul
sections.text:
A maul is a sledgehammer. It can be used as a two-handed martial weapon, but is too heavy and unwieldy to be used in one hand without Exotic proficiency. 8 lbs, bludgeoning damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x2.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d10/x3.

sections.heading: Pick, Heavy
sections.text:
The heavy pick is a mattock or pickaxe, which also supersedes the dire pickCW. 8 lbs.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x3.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x4.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d8/x4, feat (Scything Blow).

sections.heading: Pick, Light
sections.text:
The light pick, or horseman’s pick, is designed to allow a skilled user to penetrate armor, despite its light weight. The pick head is often backed by a light hammer (q.v.). Examples include the Scythian sagaris and the Polish nadziak. 2 lbs.

Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x3.Martial:  Light melee, 1d4/x4.Exotic: Light melee, 1d4/x4, feat (Deft Blow).

sections.heading: Pick, Military
sections.text:
The military pick, crowbill, or martel-de-fer, is a heavier version of the light pick, ideal for penetrating armor in the hands of a skilled user. The head of the pick is often backed by a warhammer. 4 lbs.
Simple:  One-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x3.Martial:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x4.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d6/x4, feat (Crushing Blow); or one-handed melee, 1d8/x4.

sections.heading: Polearms
sections.text:
This is a varied group of weapons, many of which also belong to other weapons groups. The following polearms are fully described in the sections listed:
Weapon | Section (Group Header)
Flail, Pole | Flails and Whips
Glaive | Axes
Halberd | Axes
Hammer, Lucerne | Hammers and Picks
Long Spear | Spears
Morningstar | Bludgeons
Ranseur | Spears

sections.heading: Guisarme
sections.text:
A guisarme is a modified pruning hook, an 8-foot-long shaft with a blade and a hook mounted at the tip. The curve and/or hook of the blade allows the guisarme to be used as a tripping weapon. Such weapons as the bill and Welsh hook, and the long-handled Thracian rhomphaia, are similar enough that they can use the same basic statistics. 9 lbs, slashing damage.
Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x2, reach, trip.Martial:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, reach, trip.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d10/x3, feat (Shorten grip), reach, trip.

sections.heading: Lajatang
sections.text:
A lajatang is a rare and unusual double weapon found only in the hands of martial artists skilled in its use. It consists of a three- to five-foot shaft with a crescent blade fitted at each end. The “monk’s spade” can use these stats, as well as such fantasy weapons as the crescent scytheSSt, the thri-kreen gythkaShS, and the orc double axeUE. 7 lbs, slashing damage.

Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x2.Martial: Two-handed double melee weapon, 1d8/x3.Exotic: Two-handed double melee weapon, 1d8/x3, feat (Two-Weapon Fighting or Whirlwind Strike), finesse.

sections.heading: Mancatcher
sections.text:
This polearm consists of two curved metal bands that close around or snag a target when you attack, allowing you to bind an opponent. A mancatcher is built to capture a creature of a particular size category (e.g., Medium) and doesn’t work on creatures of the wrong size. The kuo-toa “pincer staff” is a mancatcher, as is the Japanese sasumata.
A wielder with Exotic proficiency can make a touch attack to hit an opponent and a combat maneuver check to grapple him (without the –4 penalty for not having two hands free); success means you and the target are grappled. Once the target is grappled, you can perform a move or damage grapple action against him. The mancatcher has hardness 10 and 5 hit points; it requires a DC 26 Strength check to break it. If you drop the mancatcher, the target can itself by spending two partial actions. 8 lbs, piercing damage.
Simple: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d2, reach.Martial: Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d2, reach, entangle.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d2, reach, grapple.

sections.heading: Slings
sections.text: Slings use leverage to hurl missiles with greater force. Unless otherwise noted, sling weapons apply the wielder’s Strength modifier to damage. As with other projectiles, however. the user’s Wisdom modifier applies to attack rolls.

sections.heading: Atlatl
sections.text:
The atlatl, or spear thrower, in its most basic form is a stick used as a lever to throw a dart (q.v.) or javelin (q.v.) with more force. The Australian woomera, Eskimo nuqaq, Macedonian kestros, and the leather Roman amentum use these statistics. The “Swiss Arrow” or “Yorkshire Arrow” is essentially a pre-loaded, single-shot atlatl. 1 lb., piercing damage.

Simple: One-handed projectile (30 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2, reload 2 move actions.Martial: One-handed projectile (40 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload 1 move action.Exotic: One-handed projectile (50 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload 1 move action, feat (Far Shot).

sections.heading: Sling
sections.text:
A sling is little more than a leather cup attached to a pair of strings. Your Strength modifier applies to damage rolls when you use a sling, just as it does for thrown weapons. You can fire, but not load, a sling with one hand. Loading a sling requires two hands and provokes attacks of opportunity. 0 lbs., bludgeoning damage.
Special: You can hurl ordinary stones with a sling, but stones are not as dense or as round as bullets. Thus, such an attack deals damage as if the weapon were designed for a creature one size category smaller than you.

Simple: One-handed projectile (50 ft.), 1d4/x3, reload 2 move actions.Martial: One-handed projectile (60 ft.), 1d6/x3, reload 1 move action.Exotic: One-handed projectile (60 ft.), 1d8/x3, reload swift action; or one-handed projectile (60 ft.), 1d6/x3, reload 1 move action, feat (Staggering Strike).
Synergy: If you have at least Martial proficiency with the sling and with Flails and Whips, you can use a loaded sling exactly as if it were a light flail (including any feats and/or talents you have that normally apply to the light flail). This supersedes the Sling FlailUC feat.

sections.heading: Sling, Staff
sections.text:
Made from a specially designed sling attached to a pole, a staff sling can be used by a proficient wielder to devastating effect. Your Strength modifier applies to damage rolls when you use a staff sling, just as it does for thrown weapons. Exotic proficiency supersedes the war slingRW. 3 lbs, bludgeoning damage.
Special: You can hurl ordinary stones with a staff sling, but stones are not as dense or as round as bullets. Thus, such an attack deals damage as if the weapon were designed for a creature one size category smaller than you and you take a –1 penalty on attack rolls.

Simple: Two-handed projectile (40 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x3, reload 1 full round.Martial: Two-handed projectile (80 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x3, reload 2 move actions.Exotic: Two-handed projectile (80 ft.), 1d8/x4, reload 1 move action.

sections.heading: Spears
sections.text: Unless otherwise noted, all spears deal piercing damage.

sections.heading: Harpoon
sections.text:
The harpoon is a heavy, barbed throwing spear with a socketed head. It is generally attached to a line so that it can be retrieved on a miss (a partial action), and/or used to drag prey to the wielder on a hit. It can be used in melee with a -4 competence penalty. 8 lbs.

Simple: Two-handed throwing (10 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d10/x2.Martial:  Two-handed throwing (20 ft.), 1d10/x2, entangle.Exotic:  One-handed throwing (30 ft.), 1d10/x3,  entangle, feat (Impaling Attack).

sections.heading: Javelin
sections.text:
The javelin (including the Frankish angon, Iberian falarica, and Middle Eastern/African assegai) is a throwing spear. Roman armies had at least three versions: the lancea, the verutum, and the heavier pilum. Thrown javelins are subject to the same breakage chances as arrows. 4 lbs. A javelin can be used in melee as a short spear (q.v.) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks (and no Exotic usage in melee).
Simple:  One-handed throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/x2.Martial:  One-handed throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/x3.Exotic: One-handed throwing (30 ft.), 1d8/x3. If you hit a shield-using opponent with a javelin, he loses the AC bonus from that shield until he takes a partial action to pry out the remnants.

sections.heading: Lance
sections.text:
The lance is a long spear, designed for use from horseback. If used from the back of a charging mount, the lance deals double damage on a successful hit, but cannot be used two-handed in that case. In addition to the familiar knight’s lance, the xyston used by Macedonian cavalry (hertairoi) is a lance, as is the Achaemenid kontos. 10 lbs.

Simple:  Two-handed melee with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d8/x2, brace, reach.Martial: Two-handed melee (and one-handed melee, but attacking this way costs two partial actions), 1d8/x3, brace, reach.Exotic:  One-handed melee, 1d8/x3 (1d12/x3 vs. Large and larger opponents), brace, reach.

sections.heading: Ranseur
sections.text:
A trident-like polearm designed to parry and disarm weapons at a distance. The partisan, spetum, corsèsque, half-pike, military fork, tiger fork, spontoon, and “Bohemian ear-spoon” are essentially similar, as is the Japanese kama-yari and Korean dangpa. 6-7 feet long, 4-6 lbs.

Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x2, brace, reach.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, disarm, reach.Exotic: Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, disarm, feat (Shorten Grip), reach, trip.

sections.heading: Spear
sections.text:
A war spear can be used in both hands as a simple weapon, or in one hand (or thrown) as a martial weapon. Examples include the Chinese qiang, Hoplite dory, Japanese yari, Roman hasta, Tamil vel, and the Viking spear. Minor variations, such as the trident, do not merit separate statistics.
Wielders with the Two-Weapon Fighting feat can use a spear as a double weapon, striking with the butt end as if it were a staff. 4 lbs.

Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace.Martial: One-handed melee and throwing (10 ft.), 1d8/x3, brace.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, and feat (Lunge); and two-handed melee 1d12/x3, brace, finesse or feat (Lunge); and one-handed throwing (20 ft.) 1d8/x3.

sections.heading: Spear, Long
sections.text:
In essence, a spear with a longer shaft, allowing it to be used as a reach weapon. Examples include the Aztec tepoztopilli, Korean jangchang, and Macedonian sarissa, and, for especially long shafts, the pike and awl pike (Ahlspiess). Exotic usage includes most pike options, and also supersedes the great spearCW and the dwarven war pikeRS, if the greater damage die is selected instead. 6 lbs.
Simple:  Two-handed melee, 1d8/x2, brace, reach.Martial: Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, reach.Exotic: (a) Two-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, feat (Lunge), reach; or (b) two-handed melee, 2d6/x3, brace, reach; or (c) one-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, reach.

sections.heading: Spear, Short
sections.text:
The short thrusting spear (“ixwa”―named for the sound made when it was withdrawn from a wound) was made famous by the Zulu actions against the British at the Battle of Isandlwana in 1879, and the subsequent defense at Rorke's Drift. This category of weapon also includes the “halfspear.” The Flemish goedendag and French plançon à picot use these stats when used for thrusting (otherwise treat as heavy clubs). 3 lbs.
The sang kauwOA is essentially a double weapon combining the short spear and cutlass (q.v.), with the possible addition of a built-in buckler.
Simple:  One-handed melee, 1d6/x2, brace.Martial: One-handed melee and throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/x3, brace, finesse.Exotic: One-handed melee, 1d8/x3, brace, finesse, and feat (Hammer the Gap or Spearfighter); and one-handed throwing (20 ft.), 1d8/x3.

sections.heading: Axe, Throwing
sections.text: A throwing axe, such as the francisca, is a hand axe (see full description under “Axes”). Martial Weapon Proficiency with throwing weapons grants ranged (throwing) proficiency at the Martial level, but no melee proficiency, with the hand axe.

sections.heading: Bolas
sections.text:
A bolas is a pair of weights, connected by a thin rope or cord. You can use this weapon to make a ranged trip attack against an opponent. You can't be tripped during your own trip attempt when using a bolas. 2 lbs, bludgeoning damage (or piercing damage with barbed bolas)

Simple: One-handed throwing (10 ft.) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x2, nonlethal.Martial: One-handed throwing (10 ft.) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x2, entangle, nonlethal.Exotic: One-handed throwing (10 ft.), 1d4/x2, entangle, trip, lethal or nonlethal.

sections.heading: Boomerang
sections.text:
The boomerang is primarily a hunting tool, but it is not uncommon to carry these versatile weapons into battle. A boomerang (or hunting stick or “kylie”) is made of wood and is flat, with a long haft, a pronounced forward curve, and a sharp backward bend at the head. The Maasai throwing club (orinka or rungu) and similar weapons can also use these statistics. 1 lb., bludgeoning.
Simple: Light throwing (20 ft.) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x2.Martial: Light throwing (30 ft.), 1d4/x2 and returns to thrower on a miss.Exotic: Light throwing (40 ft.), 1d4/x2, feat (Staggering Strike), and returns to thrower on a miss; or light throwing (50 ft.), 1d6/x2.

sections.heading: Chakram
sections.text:
The chakram is an elegant and highly portable thrown weapon. It is a flat, open-centered metal discus with a sharpened edge; however, any exotic throwing wedge, such as the thri-kreen’s “chatkcha,” can be treated as a chakram. You can also use these stats for any of the various multi-bladed African throwing knives such as the mambele or the hunga munga (or the “kapok” from the movie The Beastmaster). The annulatPnH and the Varisian starknifeUE can also be treated as chakrams. 1 lb., slashing damage.
Any attempt to wield a chakram as a melee weapon requires a DC 15 Reflex save to avoid cutting yourself on the blade (half damage, no Strength modifier). You do not need to make this save if wearing heavy armor or a gauntlet.

Simple: Light melee or throwing (10 ft.) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d6/x2.Martial: Light melee (1d6/x2) with a -4 competence penalty to attacks, and throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/19-20.Exotic:  Light melee (1d6/x2) and throwing (20 ft.), 1d6/18-20.

sections.heading: Dagger, Throwing
sections.text: The throwing dagger is simply a dagger (see full description under “Light Blades”) that is balanced for throwing. Martial Weapon Proficiency with throwing weapons grants throwing proficiency at the Martial level with the dagger, but no melee proficiency. For exotic proficiency, the thrown option (1d4/19-20/x3 applies).

sections.heading: Dart
sections.text:
More similar to a lawn dart than a pub dart, this is a throwing weapon, smaller and lighter than a javelin, typically fletched like an arrow. The head is often weighted with lead; thus the Roman name plumbata. For the sake of convenience, other small throwing weapons such as shuriken can be modeled using these statistics as well. Half a pound; piercing damage.
Simple:  Light throwing (20 ft.), 1d4/x2.Martial:  Light throwing (20 ft.), 1d4/x3.Exotic: Light throwing (20 ft.), 1d4/x3, feat (Manyshot).

sections.heading: Hammer, Throwing
sections.text: The throwing hammer is simply a light hammer (see full description under “Hammers and Picks”) that is balanced for throwing. Martial Weapon Proficiency with throwing weapons grants throwing proficiency at the Martial level with the throwing hammer, but no melee proficiency.

sections.heading: Javelin
sections.text: See full description under “Spears” (q.v.).

sections.heading: Net
sections.text:
A net is used to entangle enemies. When you throw a net, you make a ranged touch attack against your target; on a hit, the target is entangled. A net must be folded to be thrown effectively; after the net is unfolded, you take a –4 penalty on attack rolls with it unless you have Exotic proficiency.
An entangled creature can escape with a DC 20 Escape Artist check (a full-round action). The net has 5 hit points and can be burst with a DC 25 Strength check (also a full-round action). A net is useful only against creatures within one size category of you.
For the sake of simplicity, you can use these statistics for a lasso as well.
Simple:  A person with only Simple proficiency cannot use a net effectively in combat.Martial: Two-handed throwing (10 ft.), entangle, refold 1 full round.Exotic:  One-handed throwing (10 ft.), entangle and special (+2 to attacks vs. entangled opponent with a weapon held in your other hand), refold 2 partial actions.
Synergy: If you have Exotic proficiency with the net and also have the Improved Trip feat, you treat the net as if it had the Trip quality. If you have the Improved Weapon Maneuvers feat, you treat the net as if it had the Disarm quality. Exotic net proficiency (and the synergy effects) supersedes the Net Adept, Net and Trident, and Net Maneuvering featsUC.

sections.heading: Rock
sections.text:
Johnson jerked his head in her direction, and it was then I realized Terri had stooped down and got a rock, and she threw it. It was like the day she killed that bird. Her aim was true. It smote Johnson on his forehead, knocking off his hat, and he sort of went up on his toes and fell back, flat as a board, right by that hole we had dug.
I looked down at Johnson. He had a big red welt on his forehead, and it was already starting to swell into a good-sized knot.
“Girly, my ass,” Terri said as she came up.
I bent down and took hold of his wrist, but didn’t feel a pulse.
“Terri, I think you done killed him.”
“I was trying to. Did you hear the way it sounded when it hit him?”
“Like a gunshot,” I said.
―Joe R. Lansdale,
“Driving to Geronimo’s Grave” (2018)
A character with proficiency and strength can hurl rocks or even iron shot puts to devastating effect. (In the Pathfinder rules, a rock is defined as “any large, bulky, and relatively regularly-shaped object made of any material with a hardness of at least 5.”) Exotic proficiency supersedes the giant’s “rock throwing” extraordinary ability. 15 lbs., bludgeoning.
Simple: One-handed throwing (10 ft.) with -4 competence penalty to attacks, 1d4/x2.Martial:  One-handed throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x2; and two-handed throwing (10 ft.), 1d6/x2.Exotic:  One-handed throwing (range dependent on thrower’s size and Strength; see below), 1d6/x2; or one-handed throwing (10 ft.), 1d8/x3.
Size | Range Increment
Medium or smaller | 5 ft. x St bonus
Large | 10 ft. x Str bonus
Huge | 15 ft. x Str bonus
Gargantuan | 20 ft. x Str bonus
Colossal | 25 ft. x Str bonus
In the deserts of Bailakash lives a species of insects that throw individual grains of sand with devastating effect.

sections.heading: Magic Items and Wealth
sections.text:
And as they rode, Arthur said, “I have no sword…” So they rode till they came to a lake, which was a fair water and broad, and in the midst of the lake Arthur was ‘ware of an arm clothed in white samite, that held a fair sword in that hand.
―Sir Thomas Malory, Le Morte d’Arthur (1470)
An effort has been made to decouple magical gear from monetary wealth. This allows characters to spend fortunes on castles, lavish parties, or whatever else they desire, without automatically falling behind their peers in terms of personal power. To this end, a number of the new feats and class features are intended to supersede the “standard” items (cloaks of resistance, belts of physical might, and the like). In addition, “wealth by level” as a measure of magical gear is, if not abolished, at least modified heavily enough that material wealth no longer translates directly to magical power.
Magic Item Economics: Because of the time and effort it takes to craft magical items (not to mention the investment of personal numen—see below), major magical items are not openly for sale for mere money―a +5 sword can do things that any number of gold coins can’t do, and adding more tons of gold doesn’t change that. Major magic items generally must be bartered for with items of equivalent value: other magic items, souls trapped in items or in the form of larvae, the stuff of raw chaos crystallized into gems (such as those used in Steven Brust’s “pre-empire sorcery”), etc. In general, magical gear worth over 10,000 gp or so (based on the diamond value required for a resurrection spell) cannot be purchased for mundane coin under almost any circumstances.
This cash limit does not apply to non-magical items and goods such as sailing ships or castles: only to major magical items and certain special materials.
Magical Items as Class Features: In some cases, you receive enhancements to items directly as a class feature. Examples include the fighter’s Personal Weapon talent; the prestige paladin’s bonded armor, holy symbol, or weapon; the wizard’s bonded item. Unless otherwise noted, these items do not count against your personal numen (see below). However, they also do not generally function for people other than you, so that selling or trading them is pointless.

sections.heading: Personal “Mojo” (Numen)
sections.text:
Even with a shift in currency expectations, you’re still in a situation in which wealth (of whatever sort) directly buys power, and the hope is to diminish that. As a proposed alternative, irrespective of actual monetary wealth (of any kind) available for spending, a given character can only maintain a personal equipage of magical gear set by the limits of his or her personal power, or “numen” (author’s note: I preferred “mojo” as the term for this, but was outvoted).
Each item “costs” a certain amount of numen to bind to one’s use; items not bound to a character can be retained only temporarily (see “Maximum,” below). To bind an item to yourself, you must spend an amount of numen equal to the gold piece value of the item. Magical items obtained in excess of your maximum numen limit cannot be bound to you.
Character Level* | Numen (or gp value equivalent of gear):
Min. | “Par” | Over. | Max.
1st | 0 | 500 | 1,500 | 2,000
2nd | 780 | 1,000 | 2,000 | 3,000
3rd | 1,650 | 2,700 | 3,300 | 6,000
4th | 2,400 | 5,400 | 5,100 | 10,500
5th | 3,450 | 9,000 | 7,000 | 16,000
6th | 4,650 | 13,000 | 10,500 | 23,500
7th | 6,000 | 19,000 | 14,000 | 33,000
8th | 7,800 | 27,000 | 19,000 | 46,000
9th | 10,050 | 36,000 | 26,000 | 62,000
10th | 12,750 | 49,000 | 33,000 | 82,000
11th | 16,350 | 66,000 | 42,000 | 108,000
12th | 21,000 | 88,000 | 52,000 | 140,000
13th | 27,000 | 110,000 | 75,000 | 185,000
14th | 34,800 | 150,000 | 90,000 | 240,000
15th | 45,000 | 200,000 | 115,000 | 315,000
16th | 58,500 | 260,000 | 150,000 | 410,000
17th | 75,000 | 340,000 | 190,000 | 530,000
18th | 96,000 | 440,000 | 245,000 | 685,000
19th | 123,000 | 580,000 | 300,000 | 880,000
20th | 159,000 | 760,000 | 240,000 | 999,999
* 	For monsters with racial HD (other than racial paragon levels, etc.) or characters with levels in an NPC class, use total CR instead.
An unfortunate by-product of this system is the need to track the total value of your items. If that’s too much of a pain for a given group, they can simply accept the two-tiered currency system and hand-wave the rest in terms of bartering and so on, and the game can still work―but it’s more effort for the referee, who in essence is stuck tracking your items for you in order to balance encounters appropriately.
A scroll or potion that is created, found, or purchased, and that is consumed almost immediately (not copied into a spellbook), does not count against your total gear. However, a character who keeps one or more potions or scrolls “on hand” must tally those items against his or her limits.
