Feats

An item that allows the user to use a feat is priced based on the prerequisites for use. The base cost is 2,000 numen x the minimum base attack bonus or number of skill ranks, etc. needed to gain the desired feat effects.

  • For metamagic feats, the maximum final spell level is limited by the effective caster level of the item that you pay for. For example, a 10,000-numen metamagic item would not accommodate spells with a final (modified) level greater than 5th.
  • For feats that grant additional uses of class features (e.g., Extra Channeling), the cost is 2,000 numen x the minimum level needed to gain the final number of uses. For example, Extra Channeling grants 2 additional uses per day; if you can already channel energy 3/day, the cost would be 18,000 numen (channeling energy 5/day requires a 9th level caster).
  • For feats that grant additional rounds per day, the cost is 2,000 + (1,000 x the number of additional rounds after the first).

As always, feats such as Weapon Specialization that grant numerical bonuses cannot be added this way. Numerical bonuses are always priced based on the bonus, as described above, and never as a feat or spell.

Example: A magic mace that allows the use of the Crippling Strike feat (Str damage only, BAB +6) would cost 6 x 2,000 = 12,000 numen. The same item allowing use of the same feat, but dealing Str, Dex, and Con damage (BAB +16) would cost 32,000 numen instead. The user must meet the prerequisites, unless the magic item cost is increased to cover those as well (by adding another feat, etc.).

For non-metallic weapons and armor, use the Druid of Earth and Metal feat (Chapter 3, under Druid), for a base cost of 2,000 numen. In addition, these items are not susceptible to heat metal, shocking grasp, rusting grasp, etc.; treat this aspect as a spell effect (see below): resist energy (2nd level) x CL 3rd x 1,000 x 1 (contingent spell effect) = 6,000 numen. The total cost is 8,000 numen.

More examples of feat-based weapon properties, etc. are provided in Appendix A.

Continuous items/spells radiate the applicable effects at all times. For example:

  • A lantern of revealing is simply a permanent invisibility purge spell placed on a lantern; the cost is 3 (spell level) x 5 (caster level) x 1,000 (continuous effect) x 2 (duration 1 min./level) = 30,000 numen—exactly that listed in the CRB.
  • A ring of energy resistance uses the 2nd level resist energy spell (2nd level x CL 12th x 1,000 x 1.5 (duration) = 36,000 numen for resist energy 30. Smoothing the progression yields a value of 1,200 numen per point of resistance (i.e., 12,000 numen for resistance 10, etc.).
  • For things that can move really fast when driven or ridden, compare the following:
    • Celerity: 0 level x CL 1sr x 500 (use-activated) x 2 (1 min./level) = 500 numen for a +10-ft. enhancement to speed.
    • Wind Walk: 6th level x CL 11th x 500 x 1 = 33,000 for 600 ft. speed = 275 numen per 5 ft.

These prices are more or less comparable to 250 numen per +5 ft. of speed, and that pricing is assumed in these rules.

Use-activated: These sorts of items must be wielded or otherwise intentionally employed for the effects to come into play. Cost is half that of continuous spell-effect items (500 x spell level x caster level x duration modifier). Most magic weapon effects (see below) are priced this way. In addition, magical strongholds, etc. (which are of little use unless inhabited) generally use this pricing as well.

FAQ: “Why are the costs so low?” Observant players will note that the continuous-effect costs are half those listed in the Pathfinder core rules for custom items; use-activated costs are one-fourth of the values listed. A: This pricing not only better reflects most of the example item prices in the Pathfinder Core Rulebook, but it also allows all characters, not just casters, to benefit from the wealth of spells available. In addition, martial characters are far more gear-dependent than casters; this system makes that gear somewhat easier to come by.

Adjusted Spell Levels: In some cases, spell levels can be reduced using metamagic (Chapter 8). Items using spells modified in that manner may have certain additional restrictions:

  • Restricted Spell: Magic items with caster-restricted spells generally must be crafted by someone meeting the same restrictions. For example, a magic item providing the effects of a good hope spell (restricted to bards) can only be crafted by a bard. If a non-bard wishes to obtain such an item through expenditure of numen, it must be worked into the ongoing campaign story appropriately and is subject to referee approval.
  • Ritual Spell: Continuous-effect magic items made using spells with this feat are suppressed for longer periods of time if dispelled. A full-round spell (-1 level) is suppressed for twice as long as normal. A full ritual spell (-2 levels) is suppressed for the normal amount of time plus the full (ritual) casting time.

Armor and Weapon Properties

In keeping with the lack of a markup on multiple properties for a single item, the “+1 enhancement bonus equivalent” pricing scheme has been exchanged for a menu of flat costs, generally using the use-activated spell effect rules above. This allows multiple minor properties (flaming, keen, returning, etc.) to be added without geometrically increasing the cost of the item, whereas more powerful effects (i.e., higher-level spells) do greatly increase item pricing.

Duration Multipliers: When creating use-activated spell effect weapons, a straight duration multiplier is not appropriate for effects such as hold monster, that are applied instantaneously to the target but then last for some period of time. In such cases, use the instantaneous (x8) multiplier, not the effect duration. Given the high costs this typically generates, most such effects are made contingent (e.g., as Strikes); as described in the following section.

Energy Weapons: The caustic, flame, frost, and shock weapon properties (+1 bonus cost in the Pathfinder rules) are built using the spells rules in Chapter 8: Acid splash (or jet of flame, etc.; 0 level) + Channel Spell (+1 level) + Reach Spell (close to touch; -1 level) = 0 level x CL 1st (1d6 damage only) x 500 x 8 (instantaneous duration) = 2,000 numen. This allows the flaming property to be added to weapons with higher enhancement bonuses without pushing the cost up unreasonably.

Other Properties as Spell Effects: Other examples are handled similarly to energy weapons. A few of the most common are provided here; a large number of others can be found in Appendix A.

  • Animated (shield): Not applicable as a spell effect; numerical bonus pricing rules (see above) always take precedence over spell effect rules.
  • Blessed: 1st level bless weapon x CL 1st x 500 x 2 (1 min./level) = 1,000 numen. Weapon is good-aligned and auto-confirms crits vs. [evil] opponents.
  • Dancing: 4th level dancing bladeCA x CL 4th (dances only 4 rounds at a time) x 900 (command-activated) = 14,400 numen.
  • Distance: 1st level longshotUC x CL 1st x 500 x 2 (1 min./level duration) = 1,000 numen; adds 10 ft. to the weapon’s range increment.
  • Fortification: 5th level shield of fortificationACG x 500 x 2 (1 min./level) = 5,000 numen per 5% (i.e., 25,000 for 25%, 50,000 for 50%, 75,000 for 75%). Because of the expansion of precision-based effects in these rules (Chapter 7), the higher pricing is more than reasonable.
  • Ghost Touch (Armor): 2nd level ghost touch armorLM x CL 3rd x 500 x 2 (1 min./level) = 6,000 numen.
  • Penetration of DR, as if made of a special material: 2nd level (non-variable) heart of the metalACG x CL 3rd x 500 x 2 (duration) = 6,000 numen.
  • Speed: 3rd level haste spell x CL 5th x 500 x 4 (1 round/level duration) = 30,000 numen (the same cost as applying a +3 weapon quality to a +1 weapon, as in the CRB).

Critical or Contingent Properties: Weapon property spell effects that activate only on a critical (e.g., the deafness effect of a thundering weapon, or the additional damage dealt by a flaming burst weapon) are priced as use-activated spell effects (see above). However, because the effect occurs only contingent on specific activation conditions, spell duration pricing modifiers do not apply. In these rules, critical-only properties are expanded so as to activate on any of the conditions normally associated with [Strike] feats (Chapter 5). Examples include the following:

  • Bane: 2nd level bladebaneUE spell x CL 6th x 500 x 1 (contingent; specific creature type only) = 6,000 numen; the weapon’s enhancement bonus increases by 2 against creatures of the appropriate type, and it deals additional force damage against them (+6d6 for one attack/rd., +3d6 each for 2/rd., +2d6 each for 3-4/rd. If the effect somehow becomes non-contingent (i.e., the creature type can be changed), then multiply by 4 (for 1 rd./level duration), for a total cost of 24,000 numen.
  • Dispelling: 0 level dispel + Channel Spell (+1 level) = 1st level x CL 5th x 500 x 1 (activated as a [strike] effect) = 2,500 numen, +500 numen per caster level above 5th. A dispelling burst weapon, with a greater dispel magic effect, would cost 6 x CL 11th x 500 = 33,000 numen, + 3,000 numen per caster level above 11th.
  • Disruption: 5th level disrupting weapon spell x CL 9th x 500 x 1 (usefulness is contingent on fighting undead) = 22,500 numen; undead take +9d6 positive energy damage (1 attack/rd.), +5d6 each for 2 attacks/rd., +3d6 each for 3 attacks, or +2d6 each for 4+ attacks, no save.
  • Ghost Touch: 3rd level ghost touch weaponSC spell x CL 5th x 500 x 1 (contingent on fighting incorporeal opponents) = 7,500 numen.

Other

Creativity is encouraged, especially in regards to ideas that have no clear rules elsewhere. This section provides a number of examples to showcase demonstrate ways to implement these sorts of ideas.

Embedded Items: Applying the tattoo itemRR spell as a continuous spell effect is a simple way to create items that are physically embedded in your body. Although the spell as written in the source material suppresses the item’s properties, that’s a holdover from the “limited item slots” paradigm in 3.0/3.5 and can be ignored in these rules. Also, while embedded items can take the form of tattoos (as the spell implies), there’s no particular reason an item couldn’t as easily be a gem embedded in your forehead, a cybernetic enhancement, an arcane symbiont, or whatever. Cost is as a 4th level spell x CL 7th x 1,000 x 0.5 (permanent duration) = 14,000 numen.

Applying this ability to your familiar allows you to emulate the Tattooed Sorcerer’s familiar tattooPC.

Enhanced Companions: A familiar, animal companion, bonded mount, etc. can be enhanced using your personal numen exactly as if it were a magical item. For example, a dog could be given a +4 enhancement bonus to Constitution for 16,000 numen, or a +2 bite for 8,000 numen, or a permanent expeditious retreat effect for 2,000 numen (see spell effects, above). In this manner, the special familiar abilities in 1st edition can be duplicated; by spending 10,000 numen, for example, a pseudodragon familiar can be made to bestow SR 15 on its master (5th level spell resistance x CL 1st x 1,000 for continuous use x 2 for duration).

Intelligent Items: There are a several ways to go about this.

  • If you have the arcane bond class feature, one option is to select a bonded object and also take the Arcane Bond feat (Chapter 5), and designate the object as your familiar. The object then gains an Intelligence score equal to 5 + half your effective master level (see Wizard, Appendix B, and also Chapter 5: Feats).
  • A 7th level character might gain the Leadership or Command Undead feat, apply the ghost template (+2 CR) to the cohort gained, and end up with a 3rd level ghost sorcerer or incarnate (effective CR 4) bound to a personal item―thus allowing the “item” to have its own intelligence and magical abilities.

Masking Objects of Power: For magical items that do not register to detect magic and/or scrying, use the continuous spell effect rules, with the contingent duration multiplier (x1) if the effect applies only to the item. Typical spell effects for this include the following:

  • 1st level magic aura x CL 1st x 25 (latent effect, applies only when detect magic used) = 25 numen (item up to 5 lbs. only; for heavier objects, add Widen Spell to the base spell). The item does not register as magical to detect magic, etc. but can still be found by scrying, locate object, etc.
  • 3rd level nondetection x CL 5th x 25 (latent) = 375 numen; the object resists location magic. The Concentration DC to pierce the protection is equal to 11 + (1.5 x CL), so increasing the CL (and therefore the cost) is often a smart investment.
  • 3rd level nondetection x CL 5th x 1,000 x 1 (1 hour/level) = 15,000 numen; protection also extends to owner as long as item held/worn.
  • Nondetection (3rd level) – Expedient Spell (+1 level) = 4th level x CL 7th x 1,000 x 1 = 28,000 numen; as above, but no check to penetrate the warding.
  • 6th level sequester x CL 11th x 1,000 x 1 = 66,000 numen; the object is both invisible and immune to detection/location spells, but cannot be used to attack.
  • 8th level mind blank x CL 15th x 25 (latent effect) = 3,000 numen; the object is immune to divinations.
  • 8th level mind blank x CL 15th x 1,000 x 1 = 120,000 numen. The object is immune to all divinations and [mind-affecting] effects, and this protection extends to anyone holding or wearing it.

Power Conduits: For when you just can’t get enough spell slots, a personal item might serve as a conduit for raw magical power from the plane of your deity, from a circle of stones at the confluence of ley lines, or whatever. A power conduit provides you with additional “spells per day” slots (Spellcasting Table 2). This costs 2,000 numen x the maximum level of spell slots x the spell capacity level. For example, a 7th level sorcerer could have an item that draws additional magical power, adding six 1st level and three 2nd level spell slots to his total, for 16,000 numen total (2,000 x 2 x 4). Note that there is no reason a fighter cannot take the Arcane Bond feat, choose a wand as a bonded item, and enhance it with this ability in order to power it.

Individual spells, activated using the item’s spell slots, can be added for 400 numen x spell level x caster level for the first ability, ¾ that for the second, and half that for additional spells thereafter (as a staff).

Prepared Spell Slots: For casting additional prepared spells, the suggested cost is 2,000 x (spell level)2 x number of spells. Thus, a 3rd level pearl of power costs 18,000 numen, and a ring of wizardry III costs 2,000 x 32 x 3 = 54,000 numen (again, bonus spells for high attributes or school are not multiplied, unless added to the cost accordingly).

Gold: Typically only used for ceremonial weapons and armor, metal equipment made from gold is fragile, heavy, and expensive. Often golden armor is gold-plated, rather than constructed entirely from gold. Gold-plated items triple the base cost of weapons and armor (this does not count against personal numen) and have the same properties as the base item. Pure gold is too soft to hold a decent edge; unless alchemically treatedMF (use the custom items rules above), edged weapons made of gold weapons take a -2 penalty to damage rolls. Untreated gold weapons also have the fragile property, gaining the Broken quality on a natural 1 on any attack roll. Gold can be fashioned into light or medium metal armor. The softness and the weight of the metal decrease the armor/shield bonus by 2, and increase the armor check penalty by 2 (unless alchemically treated). The additional weight also makes the armor count as 1 category heavier than normal (light armor becomes medium armor, medium becomes heavy), increases spell failure chances by 10%, increases armor check penalties by 3, and decreases the max Dex bonus of the wearer by 2.

Hide and Leather: The hides of various animals and monsters (not only dragons) can be crafted into armor by a skilled leatherworker. In general, armor crafted from a creature’s hide provides an armor bonus to AC equal to half the creature’s natural AC bonus.

“I wear this garb, thou fool. To keep my body warm; likewise it is as near as good as a coat of steel against a common sword-thrust.”

―Howard Pyle, The Merry Adventures of Robin Hood (1883)

  • Hides providing an armor bonus of +3 or less are made into light armor (standard leather armor is therefore assumed to be aurochs hide armor, although a normal crocodile would also be appropriate, for example). Wolfskin armor would provide a +1 armor bonus to AC, but otherwise be identical to leather armor; grizzly bear leather would provide a +3 armor bonus to AC, etc.
  • Hides providing an armor bonus of +4 or greater are medium armor, rather than light armor, and use the base mechanics listed for hide armor. “Standard” hide armor might be made from the hide of a bison or elephant. Mastodon hide provides a +5 armor bonus, bulette armor +6, etc.
  • Hides providing an armor bonus of +7 or greater are heavy armor, rather than medium or light armor, and use the base statistics for full laminar or lamellar armor (e.g., banded mail). For example, triceratops hide armor, dire crocodile scale armor, and dire sharkskin armor are exactly identical to banded mail, except they can be worn by druids (add the nonmetallic property, using the feat costs above). Armor made from the hide of an adult red dragon (+21 natural armor) would provide a +10 armor bonus to AC.

Hides of exotic creatures are generally not available on the open market; you must kill and skin the monster (the latter requires a Survival check at DC 10 + the creature’s natural AC bonus to avoid ruining it). Regardless of the size of the creature being skinned, you can make only one suit of armor from it for a creature one or more sizes smaller (smaller suits of armor use choicer bits of material to make up for the lack of sheer mass). This requires a Craft (needlework) check, at a DC equal to that of the base armor + twice the AC bonus above normal.

The cost and characteristics of exotic hide armors are handled by assuming the armor is magical (+1 bonus per AC above 2 for light armors, above 4 for medium armors, and above 7 for heavy armors). For example, armor made from the plates of the tarrasque (+17 armor bonus) would be equivalent to +10 laminar armor, for a cost of 100,000 gp for the enhancement bonuses + 8,000 gp (nonmetallic) = 108,000 numen.

Steel: Steel is the standard material used for fabricating metal armor and weapons in human and dwarven lands. When calculating custom materials costs, steel is generally used for “base” stats for items normally made from metal.

Stone: The wood elves of Estren do not work metal; their weapons, when not made entirely of wood, are often of stone―light and one-handed bludgeoning weapons, daggers, axe-heads, spearheads, and arrowheads can all be made of stone. Sling bullets can be made of heavy ceramic rather than lead. In some cases, edged weapons can be simulated by setting obsidian into wood; the macuahuitl is essentially a stone bastard sword. Stone weapons and armor are made using the Craft (lapidary) skill rather than the Craft (smith) skill.

Stone weapons are easier to sunder than their steel counterparts, as shown in the table. Also, they have the “fragile” quality and are prone to breaking during normal use. When you roll a natural 1 on an attack roll with a stone weapon, the weapon gains the Broken condition. Stone weapons cost a quarter of what base items of their type do, and weigh 75% of what base items of their type do. If you have at least Martial proficiency with a stone weapon and score a critical threat, you can intentionally break the weapon (giving it the broken condition) in order to confirm the crit without rolling; this supersedes the Disposable Weapon featUC.

Alchemically-treated stone armor is available as a breastplate, half-plate, or full plate only. Weight is roughly 150% normal, and movement speed is reduced to 15 feet for those with a base speed of 30 ft. (creatures with a 20-ft. speed have their movement rates reduced to 10 ft.). Cost is the same as for normal (steel) armor of the same category. Armor crafted from seashells or the like can be treated as stone armor.

Wood: Wood is used for the hafts of axes, the shafts of arrows, etc; clubs, staves, and so on are also typically made of wood. Wood can come in exotic types and be alchemically-treated in a variety of ways, as described below.

Because wooden armor and shields can be used by druids, they receive no numen cost discount for their lower hardness and hit points. Likewise, wood is a standard material for many types of weapons (clubs, staves, axe handles, etc.), so no numen discount is provided.

Special Materials

Special materials such as mithral and adamantine are simulated using the rules for designing custom items, above. Examples, with calculations for costs, are provided here. The materials listed here are not meant to be representative of all possible materials; new ones can be designed using the “Designing Custom Items” rules above. Unless otherwise noted, special materials costs are tallied against a character’s numen (see above). Not all special materials are freely available, particularly costly ones; referee approval is needed.

In addition to the materials listed here, a large number of special materials are described in Appendix 6a.

Adamantine: This ultra-hard metal adds to the quality of a weapon or suit of armor. Adamantine is black in color, and impossible to work without magical means and at least 11 ranks in Craft (smith) as a class skill. Items without metal parts cannot be made from adamantine (an arrow could be made of adamantine, but a quarterstaff could not).

Wide is the fronting gate, and, rais’d on high

With adamantine columns, threats the sky.         

Vain is the force of man, and Heav’n’s as vain,

To crush the pillars which the pile sustain.

―Virgil, The Aeneid (29-19 B.C.)

Dragonhide: Start with leather armor, scale mail, or banded armor as a base, then add an armor enhancement bonus (cost 1,000 gp x bonus squared, as normal) sufficient to bring the total AC value equal to half the natural AC bonus of the dragon from which the hide was taken. For example, armor made from the hide of an adult red dragon (+21 natural armor) would provide a +10 armor bonus to AC (equivalent to +3 banded armor). It also has the nonmetallic property (see above; 8000 gp). Dragonhide armor also provides resistance 10 to the type of energy the living dragon was immune to (10,000 gp). Total cost = enhancement bonus cost + 18,000 numen.

Force: Armor and weapons can be fabricated from pure magical force (use Spellcraft rather than Craft). Although almost indestructible by normal means, if dispelled (or brought into an antimagic field) they vanish completely for 1d4 rounds (or until removed from the field), during which time they provide no benefits. Use these guidelines for more fanciful examples as well, such as armor made of moonbeams.

  • Armor: 1,000 gp x (AC bonus squared). Although the armor provides an armor bonus, treat the cost as a magical enhancement bonus, so that you cannot stack an enhancement bonus to AC on top of the armor bonus it provides. Force armor has hardness 2 x the armor bonus, hp 5 x the armor bonus, no encumbrance or weight, no max AC, no skill check penalty, and no arcane spell failure chance. It gains the ghost touch property by virtue of being made of force.
  • Weapons: +20 alchemical bonus hardness (20,000 gp), +10 alchemical bonus to hp (400 gp), ghost touch property (7,500 gp) = 27,900 numen. Force weapons deal force damage rather than piercing, slashing, or bludgeoning damage.

Mithral: Mithral is a very rare silvery, glistening metal that is lighter than steel but just as hard; the secret of its working is known only to the eldest of high elves and mountain dwarves (requiring at least 6 ranks in Craft (smith) as a class skill). When worked like steel, it becomes a wonderful material from which to create armor, and is occasionally used for other items as well.

Mithril! All folk desired it. It could be beaten like copper, and polished like glass; and the Dwarves could make of it a metal, light and yet harder than tempered steel. Its beauty was like to that of common silver, but the beauty of mithril did not tarnish or grow dim.

―J.R.R. Tolkien, The Fellowship of the Ring (1954)

Weapons and armor made of mithral weigh half as much as their steel counterparts.

  • Armor and shields: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), armor check penalties reduced by 3 (900 gp), +2 to maximum Dex bonus (300 gp), -10% spell failure (6,000 gp), -50% weight (5,000 gp) = 13,450 numen.
  • Weapons: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), penetrate DR/silver (4,000 gp), gain Finesse property (2,000 gp; Special Weapon Finesse feat) = 7,250 numen.

Most mithral armors are one category lighter than normal for purposes of movement and other limitations. Heavy armors are treated as medium, and medium armors are treated as light, but light armors are still treated as light. This decrease does not apply to proficiency in wearing the armor. A character wearing mithral full plate must be proficient in wearing heavy armor to avoid adding the armor's check penalty to all his attack rolls and skill checks that involve moving.

In the case of mithral weapons, the lighter weight gives the weapon the Finesse special property (even if it did not already possess it). However, the light weight means that, for purposes of adding your Strength modifier to damage, two-handed mithral weapons are treated as one-handed (1x Str modifier), and one-handed mithral weapons are treated as light weapons (0.5 x Str modifier).

Silver, Alchemical: This alloy, formed by a complex process involving metallurgy and alchemy, looks exactly like silver, although it is much lighter. The material as presented here is a fusion of the alchemical silver from the Pathfinder rules and of the Qadarian “silversheen” metalPC.

  • Armor and shields: 20% weight reduction (800 gp), +1 max Dex bonus (75 gp), armor check penalty reduced by 1 (100 gp), -5% spell failure (1,500 gp), resist electricity 2 (400 gp) = 2,875 numen.
  • Weapons: penetrate DR/silver (4,000 gp), -1 enhancement penalty to damage (-200 gp; optional) = 4,000 (or 3,800) numen.

Steel, Damascus: The special Wootz ore (containing vanadium and other trace elements) used in this steel, along with the secret methods of crucible forging, result in carbon nanotubes within the forged metal. In addition to making this steel far stronger than normal, it produces a “watered” pattern when forged. The ore and forging techniques required for Damascus steel are known only in Bailakash and eastern Aramni.

  • Light armor and shields: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), +5 alchemical bonus to hp (100 gp) = 1,350 numen.
  • Medium armor: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), +10 alchemical bonus to hp (400 gp) = 1,650 numen.
  • Heavy armor: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), +15 alchemical bonus to hp (900 gp) = 2,150 numen.
  • Edged Weapons: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness (1,250 gp), +5 alchemical bonus to hp (100 gp), +1 enhancement bonus to damage (200 gp) = 1,550 numen.

Steel, Spring: Spring steel is a high-carbon, silicon-alloy steel with a very high yield strength. Crossbows (and prodds) constructed using spring steel can carry a higher mechanical strength than normal, but at an increased cost. For mechanical Strength scores higher than the defaults shown above, simply apply the additional cost formula for enhancement bonuses to damage. Thus, a crossbow dealing an additional +5 damage (e.g., 1d8+10 for a heavy crossbow) would cost 5,000 numen (52 x 200 gp).

Wood, Darkwood: This rare magic wood is as hard as normal wood but very light. Items not normally made of wood or only partially of wood (such as a battleaxe or a mace) either cannot be made from darkwood or do not gain any special benefit from being made of darkwood. Darkwood can be made into ironwood (q.v.), but the additional costs stack.

  • Armor and shields: -40% weight (3,200 gp), armor check penalty reduced by 2 (400 gp) = 3,600 numen.

Wood, Ironwood: Ironwood is a magical substance created by druids from normal wood. While remaining natural wood in almost every way, ironwood is as strong as steel, and resistant to fire. Spells that affect metal or iron do not function on ironwood (spells that specifically affect wood do affect ironwood). Ironwood allows the fashioning of wooden items (using the Craft (construction) skill) that function as steel items. Thus, wooden plate armor and wooden swords can be created that are as durable as their normal steel counterparts (but you cannot make chain weapons or chain armor from ironwood). Ironwood armor and shields are freely usable by druids.

  • Shields and weapons: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness of wood (1,250 gp), +5 alchemical bonus to hp of wood (100 gp), fire resistance 5 (5,000) = 6,350 numen.
  • Medium armor: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness of wood (1,250 gp), +15 alchemical bonus to hp of wood (900 gp), fire resistance 5 (5,000) = 7,150 numen.
  • Heavy armor: +5 alchemical bonus to hardness of wood (1,250 gp), +25 alchemical bonus to hp of wood (2,500 gp), fire resistance 5 (5,000) = 8,750 numen.

sections.heading: Standardized Spellcasting Rules
sections.text:
To avoid needless repetition of standard rules in the class write-ups, standardized casting rules are provided here. In the class descriptions for classes with spellcasting ability, relevant details are listed as needed only. In addition, some terms are clarified here.
Bonus Spells: Most casting classes provide bonus spells, such as the cleric’s domain spells, the sorcerer’s bloodline spells, etc. Some classes (e.g., the ranger) do not receive them at all. Multiclassed casters receive higher-level bonus spells if the contributing classes do (see Spell Theurgy, below).
In some instances, more than one bonus spell is listed for a particular spell level. Upon gaining a high enough spell capacity to gain a bonus spell of that level, you must choose which of the listed options is to be your bonus spell for that spell level; once selected, this cannot be changed.
Cantrips and Orisons: You learn or can prepare a number of 0-level spells (“cantrips” for arcane casters, “orisons” for divine casters), as shown in the tables. These spells are cast like any other spell, but they do not consume any slots and may be used at will.
Caster Level: This is the level at which your spells operate, used to determine duration, range, damage, and other level-dependent effects of your spells. Unless otherwise noted, your caster level for all spells and spell-like abilities is equal to your number of ranks in Concentration (not including bonuses from Skill Focus, etc., if any). It can never exceed your total number of Hit Dice, regardless of bonuses or other improvements. Your caster level is not necessarily the same as your Spell Capacity (see below).

Prepared Casting:
Then I spoke the spell, slowly and clearly, leaving out the four key words I had chosen to omit. The woods grew absolutely still about me as the words rang out. The spell hung before me like a crippled butterfly of sound and color, trapped within the synesthetic web of my personal vision of the Logrus, to come again when I summoned it, to be released when I uttered the four omitted words.
―Roger Zelazny, Blood of Amber (1986)
Clerics, archivists, and wizards must choose and prepare spells in advance. You can prepare and cast only a certain number of spells of each spell level per day. The number of spells per spell level you can have prepared at a time is shown in Spellcasting Table 1: Spells Prepared. In addition, you can prepare additional spells if you have a high spellcasting attribute score (the cleric and archivist have additional limitations on those spells). Each prepared spell can be used only once (unless a spell is prepared multiple times in different slots), until you rest and re-prepare.
You can spend 15 minutes to prepare 1 spell, or 1 hour to prepare any number of spells up to your total number of daily slots. When preparing spells, you can choose to leave one or more spell slots open. Later during that day, you can fill each open slot by taking 15 minutes to prepare a spell in it. In order to re-prepare spells in used slots, you must receive at least 8 hours’ rest and then spend the preparation time again.
Saving Throw DCs: For spells that allow saving throws, the DCs are equal to 10 + the level of the spell + your Charisma modifier. Characters with the Serenity feat may apply their Wisdom modifier instead of their Charisma modifier when calculating save DCs; wizards with the Diligent Preparation arcane bond can apply their Intelligence modifier instead of their Charisma modifier.
Spell Capacity: This is your row on the standardized spellcasting tables, which corresponds to an equivalent level of a full spellcaster in the core rules. Your spell capacity determines your spells known and spells per day, and the highest level of spells to which you have access.
Spellcasting Attribute: Each class has a single attribute that governs spellcasting, as listed in the class description. You are unable to learn, prepare, or cast spells from that class list if your attribute is less than 10 + the level of the spell. You gain additional spells prepared (if a prepared caster) or spells per day (if spontaneous) for a high spellcasting attribute (+1 per level of spells you are able to cast, to a maximum level equal to your spellcasting attribute modifier; unlike in the CRB, you do not gain multiple bonus spells of any level no matter how high your spellcasting attribute is).
Spontaneous Casting: Bards, incarnates, and sorcerers can cast any spell they know without preparing it ahead of time. You know a certain number of spells (Spellcasting Table 1: Spells Known). You can cast only a certain number of spells of each spell level per day. Your base daily spell allotment is given on Table 2: Spontaneous Spells per Day. In addition, you receive additional spells per day if you have a high spellcasting attribute score.

sections.heading: Theurgy
sections.text:
Multiclassing as a spell caster often works differently than in the core rules. Rather than tracking two separate spellcasting progressions, it is normally possible to some extent to combine progression from different spellcasting classes. For example, there are a number of talents and other class features (Chapter 3) allowing a caster to give up the normal spellcasting progression in one class in order to improve casting progression in another class.
This type of spellcasting improvement will be termed “theurgy” in these rules, after the Mystic Theurge prestige class in the core rules, and because of the linguistic similarity with the word “synergy”—spell theurgy works according to the general rules for class synergy features (Chapter 1).
Applying Theurgy: When spellcasting theurgy is used, the improvements shown in the class synergy table are applied directly to your Spell Capacity (q.v.) on Tables 1 and 2 (and not necessarily to the level in the class being advanced). For example, a bard 6 normally has a Spell Capacity of 5th (Bard Table 1). Upon gaining 6 levels in ranger and selecting the Harper Scout ranger lore (allowing your ranger levels to provide Weak synergy towards your bard casting), your new Spell Capacity would be 8th, allowing you to cast 4th level bard spells. This referral back to a standard table avoids unduly penalizing bards and other part-casters who gain improvements in those casting progressions from another such class.
Class Level: As noted in Chapter 1, when another class provides spellcasting theurgy, always use your actual number of levels in that class, not an “effective class level” obtained through feats, talents, etc.
Spell List Access: Theurgy generally grants access to both class spell lists, subject to any limitations specified for the class feature granting it. For example, the Arcane Hierophant druid (Chapter 3) can cast arcane spells only if the spell level is less than or equal to his or her arcane class level.
Stacking Theurgy: If you have more than one class providing theurgy towards a third class’ spellcasting progression, add all levels providing weak theurgy together and compare the total advancement in the appropriate column on Table 3; add all levels providing strong theurgy and check the total against the advancement on Table 3; and apply the total advancement to your Spell Capacity on Tables 1 (and 2, if applicable).
Theurgy and Bonus Spells: Classes that normally receive bonus spells, such as bloodline spells or domain spells, also allow acquisition of higher-level bonus spells when used for theurgy. Theurgy from classes without bonus spells (e.g., ranger) does not count towards acquiring new bonus spells. This is a specific change from the core rules, in which bonus spells are available to single-classed characters only.

sections.heading: Racial Spell-Like Abilities
sections.text:
Rather than have monsters acquire spell-like abilities haphazardly, a standardized mechanic is provided here. Creatures with access to suites of spell-like abilities gain them according to ranks in Concentration, so that their racial spell capacity is equal to their caster level. Spell-like abilities do not require material components, but otherwise conform to the spellcasting rules presented here.
Progression: One spell-like ability is gained at each odd-numbered rank in Concentration, to a maximum of 17 ranks. The spell level of each new spell-like ability gained is equal to half your number of ranks in Concentration (round up)—e.g., a character with 5 ranks in Concentration will have one 1st, one 2nd, and one 3rd level spell-like ability.
For creatures with skill ranks greater than their CR, the acquisition of higher-level spell-like abilities is normally limited by CR+1, rather than by ranks in Concentration. Specific exceptions are made for creatures with tightly-themed spell-like abilities, as shown in the Bestiary monster conversions.
Listing: A race receiving racial spell-like abilities will list them by spell level, much as bloodline or domain spells are listed. For example, the list of spell-like abilities for the half-celestial template might read: 1st—protection from evil, 2nd—aid, 3rd—cure serious wounds, 4th—holy smite, 5th—dispel evil, 6th—exalted raimentBED, 7th—holy word, 8th—holy aura, 9th—summon monster IX (celestials only).
Spellcasting Attribute: The default is Charisma; creatures whose spell-like abilities include mostly Divine spells might use Wisdom instead.
Uses Per Day: When the first spell-like ability of a given spell level is gained, it is usable once per day. A spell-like ability is usable 3 times per day if your number of ranks in Concentration is greater than or equal to 4 x the spell level of the spell-like ability. If your number of ranks in Concentration is greater than or equal to 6 x the spell level, you can use the ability at will, per the following table.

Vancian Magic
These rules were originally designed for a group of players who were adamant about retaining the traditional D&D structure of nine discrete spell levels, with a specific number of each usable per day—despite the fact that the 3.5 edition psionics model has proven to be better balanced and arguably more logical.
If being able to cast x number of spells per level per day “makes no sense,” think of spell levels as the various shells of electrons around the nucleus of an atom in a Bohr model; thus, “spell level” represents a quantum state, and no fractional spell levels are possible. As a spell is cast, the energy released is no longer available until the system is recharged.
As spell capacity improves, the caster is able to fill each ring (accounting for more spells per day of that level) and also gain access to higher quantum state shells (i.e., higher-level spells). In this rationalization, prepared casters earmark their slots to specific spells in advance; spontaneous casters do so on the fly. This Bohr model analogy is not exact, but will hopefully serve to provide some sort of workable rationale for the legacy D&D spellcasting system. (As an aside, positing this rationalization, I initially argued that “spell valence” was a better game term than “spell level,” but was unanimously overruled.)

sections.heading: Casting Spells in Combat
sections.text:
Casting spells in combat is far more difficult in these rules than in the core rules, as described under the Concentration skill in Chapter 4. This is ameliorated by the greater power and flexibility of spells (see especially Metamagic and Seed Spells, below), and by the fact that other characters can generally guard an allied caster by holding enough movement and attacks to intercept attacks―or if adjacent, simply by declaring that they are doing so (Chapter 7).
Spells with a listed casting time of “1 standard action” in the core rules generally require a move action to perform somatic gestures, a partial action to retrieve components or present a focus, and a partial action to speak the verbal components and direct the spell (Chapter 7).
For a long time, long after Moonglum had gone to rest, he studied the rune, learning not only how to verbalise it but also the twists of logic which he would have to understand, and the state of mind into which he must put himself if it were to be effective.
―Michael Moorcock, Stormbringer (1964)
For spells requiring an attack roll, the verbal component is spoken while aiming and firing (for rays) or attempting to deliver the touch (for touch spells). If you don't discharge a touch spell in the round when you cast the spell, you can “Hold the Charge” indefinitely, under the conditions described below. This means you can continue to attempt touch attacks round after round in an attempt to discharge the spell. If you touch anything or anyone while holding the charge, even unintentionally, the spell discharges. If you cast another spell, the touch spell dissipates. You can make one touch attempt as a partial action, or touch up to six willing allies as a full-round action.
In order to discharge a touch spell through a weapon or unarmed or natural attack, the spell must have the Channel Spell metamagic feat applied to it (see below) or else you must use the Spellstrike feat (Chapter 5).

sections.heading: Casting Spells on Other Planes
sections.text:
The rules listed above apply to Aviona and the rest of the homebrew world. In other places, magic might work differently: casting might be easier, harder, or even impossible. On Golarion, for example, spellcasting is much easier—casting a standard spell takes only one standard action, and the Concentration DC for casting defensively is a static 15 regardless of threatening opponents, as described in the CRB.
Certain planes have wildly differing rules of magic; some types of spells might work at improved efficiency, or not at all. In general, arcane casters attempting to cast unmodified spells on planes with different magical laws fail automatically. Spontaneous casters can attempt a Planar Sense check (Chapter 4) as a move action prior to casting the spell to cast normally (DC 15 + twice the level of the spell). Arcane casters who prepare spells can make Knowledge (the planes) checks while preparing their spells in order to prepare spells that function on the new plane of existence.
Clerical spells, incarnate spells, and monks’ ki powers work normally on all planes, except those with specific special magic traits that would indicate otherwise. However, most deities’ power and awareness does not extend to all planes. Clerics and archivists out of touch with their deities cannot regain spells above 2nd level. Druids’ connection to the natural world requires special adjudication; unless specific guidelines have been developed for a given plane, treat druids as clerics.

sections.heading: Special Magic Zones
sections.text:
In some places, localized warping of reality—either though massive magical trauma in the past or the impingement of another plane onto the Prime Material—can create conditions in which nonstandard spellcasting rules are used. In the simplest case, use the rules for casting spells on other planes (q.v.). For example, a temple of Graz’zt might count as being part of the Abyss, for purposes of spellcasting inside. Other common examples follow.
Dead Magic Areas: The ambient “mana” of the area has been totally depleted. Spells, spell-like abilities, and supernatural abilities do not work in a dead magic area. Creatures and objects inside the area cannot be detected using divination magic cast from outside the area, and creatures cannot teleport, plane shift, or otherwise magically travel into or out of the dead magic area, with the exception of using permanent planar portals to enter dead-magic planes.
Wild Magic Areas: Attempting to cast a spell or use a spell-like ability in a wild magic area results in a wild surgeTM2 (if that book is not available, use the table in the 3.5 edition System Reference Document or some similar table instead). Supernatural abilities are not so affected.

sections.heading: Active Spell Effects
sections.text:
Active spells that last more than 1 hour/level (such as create demiplane) are essentially magic items, and count against your maximum personal numen (Chapter 6) as if they were magic items you crafted. Use the continuous spell-effect pricing: spell level x caster level x 1,000 x duration multiplier (x1 for 1 hr./level, x1.5 for 10 min./level, x2 for 1 min,/level, x4 for 1 rd./level, x6 for 1 round, x8 for instantaneous).
If the effect remains active, but does not actually benefit you most of the time (e.g., an everburning torch), use the use-activated costing instead (spell level x caster level x 500 x duration multiplier).
You can choose to apply a caster level lower than your number of ranks in Concentration (minimum equal to the minimum caster level for that spell level), but this makes the effect correspondingly easier to dispel.
For permanent effects, another possibility is to spend a feat on the Permanent Spell feat (q.v.) instead.

sections.heading: Area-Effect Spells
sections.text:
Default area-of-effect descriptions are provided here. In some cases, these have slightly different rules than those described in the Pathfinder Core Rulebook.
Burst: A burst effect is 20 ft. in radius as a default (in a sphere, or hemisphere if you are standing on a flat surface). Bursts do not turn corners; interposing objects cast a “shadow” from the effect behind them. However, a burst that deals damage, if it destroys a barrier, can continue to expand to its full radius.
Cone: A cone appears as a triangle in plan view, with one corner at its point of origin. It extends a default of 30 ft., with a 30-ft.-long base. Cones are otherwise treated as bursts.
Cubes: The spell affects a default of one contiguous 10-foot cube/level. The result is generally a smaller volume than a burst, emanation, or spread (q.v.) (except by a caster of at least 17th level), but the fact that the area is shapeable makes up for the smaller volume.
Cylinder: A cylinder is similar to a spread, but is half the radius, and extends to 2.5 times that height (base 10’r., 50 ft. tall). It ignores obstructions within the area. A flattened cylinder has the same original radius (default 20 ft.), but a height of only 2/3 the radius (default 13 ft.).
Emanation: An emanation spell functions like a burst, except that the effect continues to radiate from the point of origin for the duration of the spell. The point of origin can be either:
A creature or object, in which case the emanation moves with that creature or object. A saving throw is applicable for an unwilling target to avoid becoming the point of origin; if successful, the spell is lost with no effect. You can apply the Personal Spell feat (Metamagic, below) to an emanation, in which case you become the point of origin.A point in space, in which case the emanation is stationary.
Line: A line extends from you out to the full range in a 5-ft. wide path. All creatures within that straight-line path are potentially affected. A line is blocked by a barrier, unless it deals hit point damage and deals enough damage to destroy the barrier, in which case it continues beyond to its full length.
Ray: You aim a ray as if using a ranged weapon, though typically you make a ranged touch attack rather than a normal ranged attack. As with a ranged weapon, you can fire into the dark or at an invisible creature and hope you hit something. You don't have to see the creature you're trying to hit, as you do with a targeted spell. Intervening creatures and obstacles, however, can block your line of sight or provide cover for the creature at which you're aiming.
Ray spells with a duration other than Instantaneous (e.g., ray of enfeeblement) generally have effects lasting that long; the ray itself is instantaneous unless otherwise noted.
Spread: Some effects, notably clouds and fogs, spread out from a point of origin. The effect can extend around corners and into areas that you can't see. Figure distance by actual distance traveled, taking into account turns the spell effect takes. When determining distance for spread effects, count around walls, not through them. You must designate the point of origin for such an effect, but you need not have line of effect (see below) to all portions of the effect.
Target: Damaging rays changed to area-effect spells allow a Reflex save for half damage, even if the original ray spell did not (for spells that originally allowed a save for partial effects, a successful save negates all effects for the Shaped version). However, no attack roll is needed; the caster simply indicates the target (line of effect applies). If you change a damaging ray to a target or area-effect spell, a saving throw for half damage is applicable, even if the ray did not allow one.
Wall: A wall is an unbroken plane or other flat shape with a default area of 100 sq. ft. (generally one 10-ft. x 10-ft. square) per level and a thickness of ½ inch per level. It can be straight (upright or flat), ring-shaped (A = 2πrh), or form a hemispherical dome (A = 2πr2):
Caster Level | Radius (Base 10-ft. Squares):
Ring (h = 10 ft.) | Dome

2nd | 3 ft. | 6 ft.
3rd | 5 ft. | 7 ft.

5th | 8 ft. | 9 ft.

sections.heading: Latent Spells
sections.text:
Latent spells that are not immediately discharged (such as explosive runes, glyph of warding, fire trap, symbol of death, etc.; see the Delay Spell metamagic feat, below) also count against your maximum personal numen (Chapter 6). The cost is as per a magic trap, potion, or other single-use magic item: spell level x caster level x 50. Some examples:
3rd level explosive runes or secret page x CL 5th x 50 = 750 numen.8th level symbol of death x CL 15th x 50 = 6,000 numen.

sections.heading: Cantrips and Orisons
sections.text: For 0-level spells that have non-instantaneous results and that are not maintained as continuous active spell effects using numen (see above), only one such effect or result from each 0-level spell can be in existence from one caster at one time. For example, in the core rules, if you cast another light spell while a previously-evoked light is still in effect, the first light winks out. This principle is extended to other applicable 0-level spells: e.g., create water, ghost sound, resistance, etc.

sections.heading: Castles and Dungeons
sections.text:
Spells (and abilities duplicating the effects of spells) with the [teleportation] descriptor cannot penetrate to an area that is entirely enclosed by more than 1 ft. of solid stone, 3 ft. of wood or earth, one inch of metal, and/or a thin coating of lead. The same restriction applies to scrying effects and most detection spells. This guideline, adapted from the Dungeonomicon (Frank and “K,” The Gaming Den), not only curtails “scry-and-fry” tactics, but also provides a rationale for the prevalence of both castles and dungeons in a game world in which dragons exist.
Kings therefore live in stone castles, not for defensibility from armies, but for secrecy; if a need to teleport or use scrying magic comes up, they can go to an outside room and open a leaded-glass window, but while inside an inner room with stone walls and a lead-lined door, their councils are protected from eavesdropping and teleporting assassins. Many wizards likewise live in stone towers with designated divining and transportation rooms open to the outside. Tombs and cultist headquarters are typically found in dungeons underground for similar reasons.
Dimension door effects within a dungeon or building itself are normally not affected, as the doorways, rooms, and corridors provide “open” pathways of effect within the complex itself. However, rooms with stone walls and thick stone or metal doors (such as all of the Tomb of Horrors beyond the Chapel of Evil and Stone Gate) would fall under these guidelines.
Specific exceptions to this guideline include discern location and teleportation circle (see below), both of which use the Irresistible Spell metamagic feat to circumvent the protection normally granted by solid materials.

sections.heading: Counterspelling
sections.text:
Counterspelling uses the preemptive action mechanics (Chapter 7); you hold an action to counterspell when an enemy caster begins to cast.
If the target of your counterspell tries to cast a spell, make a Spellcraft check (DC 15 + the spell's level) as a free action. If the check succeeds, you correctly identify the opponent's spell and can attempt to counter it. If the check fails, you can't do either of these things.
To complete the action, you must then cast an appropriate spell. You may use any spell to counterspell, but success is automatic only if you use the same spell as the one being cast, or one of equal level or greater with effects that are exactly opposite (e.g., haste vs. slow). Use of any other spell requires a Concentration check on your part with a special bonus equal to the level of the spell you are using as a counterspell. The counterspelling DC is equal to 10 + the enemy spellcaster’s Concentration bonus + the level of the spell you are attempting to counterspell.
Use of a spell from a school different from the one being cast results in a –4 penalty to your counterspelling attempt.
The Improved Counterspell feat provides a +4 bonus on all counterspelling attempts and allows counterspelling more quickly, scaling with the caster level of the counterspeller.

sections.heading: Dismissing Spell Effects
sections.text: You can end one of your own spells that has an ongoing duration by making a Concentration check to do so, as described in Chapter 4. There is no separate “(D)” notation needed for spell duration listings.

sections.heading: Player Note: Spellcasting Etiquette
sections.text:
Playing a caster is hard work, because you generally have access to a lot of spells, and are expected to know what they do without flipping through rulebooks or opening web browsers or PDF documents during the game.
If a player is asked for specifics of a spell his or her PC is casting, and is unable to provide them accurately and instantly, the spell fails. Obviously, keeping a set of index cards or sheet of notes (or an easily-opened page of notes on a handheld device) handy is therefore highly recommended.
Summoned Monster Stats: Any time you cast a summon monster or similar spell, it is your responsibility to have the correct stats on hand, without needing to flip through rulebooks or page through e-documents to look them up. If for some reason you fail in this task, the summoning spell fails as well, and has no effect.

sections.heading: Resurrection Survival
sections.text:
“I hope you didn’t go to all this trouble just to take cheap shots at me,” Ragowski said, surveying the paraphernalia that littered the floor around him. “Regardless, I’m impressed. Necromantic workings demand an obsessive’s eye for detail.”
The N’guise Working, which was the one the magicians had used to raise Ragowski, called for the eggs of pure white doves that had been injected with the blood of a girl’s first menstruation, to be cracked into eleven alabaster bowls surrounding the corpse, each of which contained other obscure ingredients. Purity was of the essence in this working.
―Clive Barker, The Scarlet Gospels (2015)
In the core 3.5/Pathfinder rules, races with long life spans may have an advantage in that they can potentially outwait most threats, letting them die of old age rather than acting directly, and there is little to discourage this outside of railroading of the plot. Re-instituting the 1st edition AD&D “resurrection survival” concept is an optional means of balancing long life spans without the need for the referee to constantly impose artificial time constraints.
“Fenario is an old kingdom, Vlad. Very old. Two thousand years, the same people, the same land.”
I didn’t comment on how short two thousand years would seem to Morrolan or Aliera, much less to Sethra; I just nodded.	―Steven Brust, Jhegaala (2008)

In this option, a character who wishes to be brought back from the dead must succeed at a Fortitude save at DC 5 + 1 per 10 years of the race’s “venerable” age up to 200, and +1 per 25 years thereafter. This translates to the following:
Race | Venerable Age | Resurrect DC
Half-orc | 60 | 11
Human | 70 | 12
Halfling | 100 | 15
Half-elf | 125 | 17
Gnome | 200 | 25
Dwarf | 250 | 27
Elf | 350 | 31
Dragon | 600 | 41
Fey/Outsider | (Immortal) | N/A
Failure on this saving throw means that the newly-resurrected creature instantly dies again and cannot be resurrected thereafter barring the use of a true resurrection, wish, or miracle. As shown in the table. creatures that are effectively immortal unless killed, such as most fey and outsiders, generally cannot be resurrected.
In a campaign in which this rule is used, players should keep a backup character or two, and the referee should encourage them to adventure independently of the primary characters, so that when they get used as replacement characters there is a reason they’re chosen by the remaining PCs (“Wait… you’re that Alodar?”).

sections.heading: Save-or-Lose Spells
sections.text:
Many spells that instantly take a combatant out of the fight on a failed save, such as hold person and slay living, have been modified so that they now deal attribute damage, with the condition applying if the attribute is reduced to 0 (Chapter 7, “Conditions”). In this manner, a failed save does not automatically knock a combatant out of the fight, but some debilitating effect occurs even on a successful save. See damage attribute, under “Seed Spells” below, for examples.
Spells that potentially impose permanent conditions (e.g., destruction, insanity, petrifaction) now generally deal attribute drain of the appropriate type. Attribute-draining spells use the damage attribute spell seed and the Crippling Drain metamagic feat (see below).
These sorts of spells are now obviously especially dangerous against creatures whose attribute scores are already reduced through fatigue or exhaustion.

sections.heading: Spell Effect Limitations
sections.text: In order to cut down the need to track myriad spell effects on characters at high levels, as an optional rule, a character or monster can be affected by a maximum number of spell levels worth of beneficial spells (“buffs”) equal to his or her CR. Buff spells causing this limit to be exceeded have no effect. Permanent spell effects from feats, class features, or bound magic items (Chapter 6) do not count against this limit.

sections.heading: Spell Resistance
sections.text:
Spell resistance can be selectively lowered against specific incoming spells, and then raised again, at will. This does not require an action. If you do not know what spell a dubious ally is casting on you (for example, by using the Spellcraft skill) you must decide blindly whether or not to allow the spell past your SR. An unconscious or dead creature cannot lower spell resistance in this way.
SR more or less follows standardized rules for dispelling magic—i.e., defeating it is an opposed Concentration check. For the sake of ease of play, it can be treated as a passive check, so that the DC of the Concentration check to defeat SR would be equal to 10 + the creature’s Concentration modifier (exclusive of Skill Focus, if any). However, monster hit dice often drastically outstrip CR, so for purposes of SR, the passive check DC is equal to 11 + 3 (class skill) + CR (in place of ranks in Concentration) + the creature’s Charisma modifier.

sections.heading: Spell Subtypes and Descriptors
sections.text:
Most spells, in addition to a school (see below) also receive a subtype—e.g., Conjuration [summoning], or Enchantment [charm]. These are determined by the spell seed(s) (see Seed Spells, below) and cannot be changed except by use of the Cross-Class Spell feat (see Metamagic Feats, below).
It is also possible for spells to have a descriptor―e.g., [acid] or [earth]. Spells dealing energy damage automatically gain the descriptor for that energy type, and some other seed spells provide a descriptor as well (for example, mage armor has the [force] descriptor).
When designing new spells that fit a certain theme, it is possible to add a descriptor appropriate to the theme of the spell. For example, for a spell incorporating the bind and invisible needle seed spells, the effects could be described as entangling pricker vines, and the spell given the [plant] descriptor, making it appropriate for inclusion in the Plant domain list (Cleric Appendix A). A spell dealing bludgeoning damage might be described as a crashing wave (and given the [water] descriptor), or as a smashing rock (and given the [earth] descriptor). For converted pre-published spells, this is assumed to be the case. For spells designed by players, referee permission is needed.

sections.heading: Spells as Weapons
sections.text: Spells that require an attack roll or touch attack roll, and deal hit point damage, are considered weapons for purposes of applying feats such as Weapon Specialization and Improved Critical. Treat all “touch attack” spells as a weapon group; together, all “ranged touch attack” spells (e.g., rays) get treated as a specific weapon type.

sections.heading: Spells Incompatible with the Revised Rules Framework
sections.text:
Considerable effort has been put into rectifying some of the problems pervasive in 3rd/3.5 edition D&D and Pathfinder. Specific areas addressed include the action economy, the standardized leadership rules (vs. the unfettered control of “magic minions”), limitations on effective caster level and reduced-cost metamagic use, and so on. Spells which violate or undo these corrections are, in general, incompatible with these house rules and should not be used with them. A few examples, with explanations, are provided here.
Arcane FusionCM: Use the Cascade Spell feat instead.
Awaken: This applies a template to the target, so that the mark of the wild rules (see Druid) for control of such a creature are more appropriate than treating the effect as an instantaneous spell.
CelerityPHII: Violates action economy.
Contingency: This spell has been replaced by the Delay Spell feat (q.v.).
Exquisite AccompanymentUM: The revised bard’s “effortless inspiration” class feature already does what this spell is meant to do.
Forced DreamME and WiddershinsRR: In general, spells and powers allowing you to go back in time and redo things represent a forced deus ex machina at best and a game-ender at worst. I do not recommend their use (especially as low as a 3rd level power, in the former case).
Learn Secret, GreaterAUG and Eternal LuckBRL: Use insight and inherent bonus pricing, respectively (Chapter 6) for numen costs.
Masterwork TransformationUM: As written, this spell not only violates masterwork item pricing rules, but also supersedes parts of the Craft skill.
Permanency: Gaining a permanent spell effect requires a feat (Permanent Spell) or investiture of personal numen, not merely the casting of another spell.
Psychic ReformationSRD: Retraining is already permissible, without using powers and paying xp.
Rary’s Arcane ConversionCM: Violates rules of the Variable Spell feat.
ShadowbardUM and Animate InstrumentCSc: Superseded; the revised bard can already begin and maintain inspirations while performing other actions.
Stalker’s SightRR2: The revised ranger can already do this with the quarry ability.
Suffer the FleshME: Violates maximum caster level cap described in Chapter 1.
Two MindsRR: Egregiously violates the revised action economy.
WithdrawUA1: Violates action economy.

sections.heading: Spells that Supersede Skills and Class Features
sections.text:
Invisibility was likewise impossible, at least as far as Flagg himself had been able to determine. Yet it was possible to make oneself… dim. It was necessary to actually hide when one was dim only if one saw someone whom one knew well―for, whether one was dim or not, these people almost always saw. Dimness was useful, but it was not invisibility.
―Stephen King, The Eyes of the Dragon (1987)
There are a number of published spells—both in the core rules and in various supplements—that render skills obsolete and otherwise supersede class features. This has the effect of allowing a caster (or anyone with a wand and the Spellcraft skill) to be a duplicate ranger, rogue, etc. It also severely devalues skills. In these house rules, many of the offending spells are modified or removed, as summarized below.
Searching and Trap-Related Spells: As noted under the detection seed spell, below, the detect secret doors spell is removed from the general wizard’s spell list. All other “automatic search” spells from alternative sources—bypass wardAUG, safe searchBEM3, spontaneous searchDr325, etc.—are removed from their respective standard spells lists and made into rogue skill tricks instead. (Alternatively, a multi-classed rogue/caster with a rogue class level greater than or equal to twice the level of the spell can add that spell back to the appropriate list.)
Spells Providing Bonuses to Skill Checks: These use the skill enhancement seed spell, as shown below and in Appendix 8A; examples include feather stepAPG, freedom of movement, spider climb, and others. In general, skill-enhancing spells and magic items should provide enhancement bonuses, so their effects do not stack. (There are metamagic feats below that allow other bonus types, but these feats also raise the level of the spell.)
Spells That Supersede Class Features: In general, class features should not be easily duplicated by spells. A prime example is find the path; tracking is the ranger’s stock in trade. The effects of the spell are therefore more limited when used by others, as shown under the detection spell seed below.  Other examples include:
Bestow Grace of the ChampionUM: This spell essentially renders the entire paladin class obsolete.Finding the CenterCA and Solicit PsicrystalSRD: Replace one of the familiar’s primary abilities.ProtégéCAd: Grants bardic inspiration.Vangal’s TouchRR: As written, this spell supersedes barbarian’s primary class feature; however, a modified version (as shown in Appendix C of the Cleric) is permissible.
New Spells: When new sources are introduced, use the above guidelines to evaluate whether to include them. For example, the guiding starAPG and deadeye’s loreUC spells would be restricted to the ranger’s spell list, as they intrude into the ranger’s area of expertise (they are shown this way in Appendix 8A).

sections.heading: Changes to Schools of Magic
sections.text: The following adjustments are made to specific schools of magic and spells therein.

sections.heading: Abjuration
sections.text:
All personal protective spells other than illusions are designated as Abjuration spells; this includes mage armor and shield. Also, all warding spells on a place or object, and spells modified (via metamagic) to do so, should be moved to the Abjuration school. This includes all forms of magic traps.
Changes to specific spells are summarized below.
Exorcism: Spells such as dispel evil and banishment can be used selectively to affect any undead, outsider, or other spirit possessing (through magic jar, malevolence, etc.) a body. This either banishes the possessing entity (if applicable) or expels it from the host (if not). Likewise, dimensional anchor can be used to trap a possessing spirit in the host’s body.
Warding Spells: Note the numen costs for active or latent spells, described above.

sections.heading: Conjuration
sections.text:
The school of Conjuration loses the [healing] sub-school (which is moved to the school of Necromancy) and also all energy/blasting spells (such as acid splash; these are moved into Evocation instead). It gains blink, ethereal jaunt and etherealness (all of which move the caster to the ethereal plane). Other specific changes are described below.
Feat Requirement: Controlling summoned beings (through summon monster, planar binding, etc.) requires the Thaumaturgy feat, (Chapter 5) which sets CR limits in the manner of the Leadership feat. Without the feat, all summoned extraplanar beings are automatically uncontrolled. Control over a summoned extraplanar being can be broken by dispel magic, greater dispel magic, or break enchantment, requiring a full round action to re-assert control (assuming the thaumaturgist has sufficient CR of control remaining).
It is still possible to bargain with and/or attempt to force uncontrolled outsiders into service, but they will pervert your instructions, undermine your intent, and in general be very hostile to you thereafter unless the payment offered far exceeds the inconvenience and difficulty of the service. This is a specific case in which written guidelines will almost always be insufficient; the referee’s maliciousness and/or perverse amusement are the only limiting factors when dealing with uncontrolled extraplanar beings, so expect the worst.
Summon Monster: Rather than providing lists of allowable summoned monsters, almost any extraplanar creature of the appropriate CR and HD for that spell level can be summoned if the correct spell is known. However, limits on controlled beings (see above) apply; any summoned monsters in excess of your Thaumaturgy allowance are uncontrolled. Prepared summon spells require you to state the being(s) to be summoned as part of the spell preparation, unless the Variable Spell metamagic feat is used (see summon under “Seed Spells,” below).
Summon Nature’s Ally: Summon nature’s allies are controlled through the mark of the wild class feature, rather than the Thaumaturgy feat. They generally share the preparation limitations of summon monster spells. If you cast a summon nature’s ally spell in a specific terrain, you can choose to forego the prepared summons and instead summon a random creature (or number of creatures, if using an Augmented spell) appropriate to that terrain. Doing so prevents any chance of summoning a porpoise into a desert, for example. If cast in a specific terrain that is one of your favored terrains, you can choose the exact creature type(s).
Teleport: Teleportation effects can be blocked by a sufficient thickness of earth or stone, as described under “Castles and Dungeons,” above.

sections.heading: Divination
sections.text:
Divination spells allowing a saving throw call for Intuition saves, rather than Will saves (Chapter 1). In addition, a number of spells within this school have been modified or removed outright; the rationale for many of these changes is given under “Spells that Supersede Skills and Class Features,” above.
Finally, a number of standard detection spells (detect magic, detect secret doors, detect undead) have been either modified or restricted, as noted under those spell descriptions (see Detection spell seed, below)
Read Magic: Rangers, as inveterate explorers, can still cast this spell as a cantrip; for all others, this spell is subsumed by the Knowledge (Linguistics) skill.
Scrying: Scrying effects (including clairvoyance) can be blocked by a sufficient thickness of earth or stone, as described under “Castles and Dungeons,” above.

sections.heading: Enchantment
sections.text:
Spells causing domination, charm, hold effects, and so on generally deal attribute damage or impose attribute penalties, as described under “Save-or-Lose” spells, above. This change affects most of the school of Enchantment; specific examples are provided below (under the damage attribute and ray of enfeeblement seed spells) and in Appendix 8A.
Also note that [charm] effects, as well as confusion and insanity, now call for Intuition saves rather than Will saves (Chapter 1).
Pet Peeve: In game rules language, the word “enchantment” applies strictly to the Enchantment school of magic, and not in any more general sense. Therefore you cannot “enchant” a mindless inanimate object (magic items are “imbued” with properties, not “enchanted” with them).

sections.heading: Evocation
sections.text:
All direct-damage “blasting” spells (e.g., acid splash, orb of force, etc.) are moved into the school of Evocation, including those designated as Conjuration in the 3.5 edition and Pathfinder rules.
The spell construction rules (seed spell + metamagic, described below) makes this one of the most versatile schools. For example, an evoker with the ray of frost spell, the versatile evocation ability, and a few metamagic feats (Reach Spell, Shape Spell) automatically “knows” (can construct) burning hands, cone of cold, and fireball as well (for example), without needing to put them in his spellbooks as separate spells.
Damage caps for evocation spells from the 3.0 edition Dungeon Master’s Guide are retained here, as summarized under “Effects of Heightening Spells,” below.

sections.heading: Illusion
sections.text:
Note that disbelief is now an Intuition save, not a Will save (Chapter 1).
Figments: Most of this sub-school can be built using a basic figment “seed spell” (see below) and metamagic.
Glamers: As with figments, most of this sub-school can be built using a basic glamer “seed spell” (see below) and metamagic.
Simulacrum: Constructing this spell from its component “seeds” and applying the standardized control rules for Leadership-like feats results in substantially less potential for abuse; refer to the simulacrum entry in the spells Grimoire (Appendix 8A).

sections.heading: Necromancy
sections.text:
Controlling Undead: Controlling undead, such as those produced by the animate dead or create undead spells, requires the Command Undead feat (Chapter 5), which functions much like Leadership for undead. If you do not have that feat (or exceed your CR cap), undead that you create or summon are uncontrolled.
Death Spells: These spells now generally deal Constitution damage or drain rather than hit point damage, as described under “Save or Lose Spells,” above. Specific examples are provided under Seed Spells (damage attribute), below.
Gems and Souls: Almost without exception, spells that interact with the soul require gems as material components. For this reason, those particular gems are not in large circulation, and count against the caster’s overflow numen (Chapter 6). The specific types of gems needed, and their values, are as follows:
Animate dead, etc.: Onyx or bloodstone worth 25 gp/HD of undead to be animated.Binding, soul bind, trap the soul, etc.: Black sapphire worth 1,000 gp per HD of the creature whose soul is to be trapped. The soul is either trapped within the gem itself, or else the gem is crushed (if the soul is to be consigned to Hell, etc.).Raise dead, resurrection, etc.: Diamond worth (spell level2 x caster level2), rounded up to the nearest multiple of 5,000 gp (e.g., 5,000 gp for a 5th level spell, 10,000 gp for 7th, 25,000 gp for 9th). Generally, the diamond is crushed during the casting.
Healing: The [healing] subschool is moved from Conjuration back into the school of Necromancy (where it was in 1st edition).
This subschool includes spells built using the spark of life and remove condition seeds (see below), which encompasses the cure wounds spells, neutralize poison, remove blindness/deafness, remove disease, the restoration spells, raise dead and resurrection, etc. (This change will please the many people inexplicably clamoring for a “white necromancer” variant.)
Negative Energy Damage: In order to keep the number of energy damage types manageable, desiccation damageSSt, disintegration damage, entropic damage, necrotic damage, etc. can be all treated as negative energy damage. See also ray of entropy under Seed Spells, below.
Restoration: This line of spells works somewhat differently; see Seed Spells (remove condition), below.
Skill Prerequisite: Use of a Necromancy [healing] spell requires a number of ranks in Heal as a class skill equal to twice the level of the spell (round up). In other words, only a character skilled in mundane healing can properly diagnose a problem and heal it with magic.

sections.heading: Transmutation
sections.text:
Because this school in the core rules covers almost any effect imaginable, spells in the existing Transmutation school that could reasonably fit into other schools should be moved accordingly. For example, the etherealness spell, which allows travel to the ethereal plane, should be moved to the Conjuration school; the pyrotechnics spell, which creates a burst of fireworks, should be moved to the Evocation school. This is reflected in the seed spells described below.
Changes to specific Transmutation spells are described below.
Haste: Because of the substantial boosts to martial prowess already inherent in these house rules, haste now specifically affects only one target (see under Celerity seed, below). The Mass Effect spell metamagic feat (q.v.) can be added to create a 6th level mass haste spell.
Mage Hand: No longer targets “only non-magical items,” so that this cantrip cannot do double duty as a ranged detect magic spell as well.
Spells Providing Bonuses to Skill Checks: As noted under “Spells that Supersede Skills and Class Features,” above.

sections.heading: Universal
sections.text:
Contingency: Rather than keeping contingent spells the same level and simply expending another spell slot, contingent spells are handled using the Delay Spell metamagic feat (see below). This means that contingent spells are higher level than non-contingent ones.
Permanency: The permanency spell is removed in favor of the Permanent Spell feat (see below).
Wish: A wish with permanent effects is in essence a continuous spell effect, and requires investment of personal numen accordingly (see Active Spell Effects, above): spell level x caster level x 1,000 x duration multiplier (if applicable). Dominating, forcing, or otherwise coercing another creature into pronouncing the wish for you does not transfer the cost to that creature. If the wish would put you over your maximum numen, it fails or backfires horribly. If you attempt to wish that subsequent wishes not carry this cost, the initial wish fails outright but still carries the numen cost.
It is recommended that the wish spell have the same effects as listed in the CRB, with the following additional uses and exceptions:
